news.originalContent:
Likud and Yashar, their parties, are scheduled to hold talks on Sunday, but will need to overcome major differences to work together.

Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has renewed his appeal for a unity government with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, casting a coalition that would keep him in power as integral to Israel’s national security.

In a video statement on Saturday, Netanyahu said his meeting with Eisenkot on Thursday “only strengthened the conviction that it is essential to form a national unity government”. He said such a government could “eliminate the Iranian threat once and for all” and claimed Tehran would “not hesitate to use nuclear weapons against us”.

Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party and the man given the first shot to form Israel’s next government by President Isaac Herzog, called Netanyahu’s appeal a “bluff”.

“Nice try, but these tricks don’t work on me. Nor on Israel’s citizens,” Eisenkot said.

But Eisenkot confirmed that Yashar and Netanyahu’s Likud Party were talking about the proposal for a shared government.

So what, if anything, would it take for them to govern together, and what other options does Eisenkot have?

In Israel’s October 27 election, the four-party bloc led by Eisenkot won 48 of the 120 seats in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament. Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc secured 53. Two Palestinian-led factions, the Joint List and Ra’am, also known as the United Arab List, won a record 19 seats between them.

Last week, Eisenkot’s bloc showed what it could do with the backing of both Palestinian-led factions, securing a 63-to-50 vote to approve the makeup of the Arrangements Committee, a panel that helps set the Knesset’s agenda while coalition talks are under way. The bloc then moved to set up temporary committees overseeing finance, foreign affairs and defence.

Eisenkot’s bloc and the two Arab-led factions hold 67 seats combined, six more than needed for an outright majority. Another possibility is a minority government backed by Ra’am’s eight lawmakers. Their support would give Eisenkot 56 votes against Netanyahu’s 53 if the Joint List’s 11 lawmakers abstained or stayed away from the confidence vote. That would allow a government to take office with fewer than 61 votes in favour, but it would depend on how all three groups voted.

But getting Eisenkot’s allies to agree to such a deal is another matter. Yair Golan, who leads the Democrats, is open to working with the Palestinian-led factions, while Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman and Together leader Naftali Bennett have rejected a coalition with Palestinians. However, both served in the government formed in 2021, when Ra’am became the first Arab party to formally join an Israeli governing coalition.

“One of Eisenkot’s main difficulties is the opposition of Avigdor Lieberman and Naftali Bennett [leaders of parties in his alliance] to relying on Arab parties,” Yasser Manna, a researcher at the Jerusalem Center for Studies on Israeli Affairs, told Al Jazeera. “This position restricts Eisenkot’s coalition options, but it does not automatically make a unity government with Netanyahu more likely. Instead, it increases the importance of negotiations with other parties, particularly the ultra-Orthodox parties.”

The other main option, which according to experts is the most likely scenario, is the Eisenkot bloc going into a coalition with both ultra-Orthodox parties in Netanyahu’s bloc, Shas and United Torah Judaism, which would take the Eisenkot bloc to 61.

Advisers from one faction of United Torah Judaism have reportedly sought a written commitment from all 48 lawmakers in Eisenkot’s bloc to pass a law exempting Jewish religious seminary students from military service and to shield it from being struck down by the High Court. Eisenkot and Lieberman are reportedly opposed to this compromise.

President Herzog gave Eisenkot until December 6 to form a government. Herzog can grant an extension of up to 14 days, which would take the deadline to December 20.

Eisenkot has left the door open to members of Netanyahu’s Likud Party and to far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party, provided they back a government led by Eisenkot and accept his programme.

“If members of Likud and the Religious Zionist Party truly believe this is a time for unity, as they told the president, I cannot conceive of any reason why they would not support a government under my leadership and the principles I have presented,” Eisenkot said at the ceremony where Herzog handed him the mandate.

Daniel Levy, a former Israeli peace negotiator and president of the US/Middle East Project, told Al Jazeera that agreeing to meet can serve both men politically. “The coalition formation period is about spin and distortion and trying to gain leverage,” he told Al Jazeera. “So you take a meeting to show that you were willing to talk, then say the other side made unreasonable demands.”

The two men know each other well. Eisenkot led Israel’s military from 2015 to 2019 and served as an observer in Netanyahu’s war cabinet during the first eight months of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. He left the emergency government in June 2024.

“I believe the relationship between Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot is marked by a deep crisis of trust that goes beyond political competition,” Manna said. “However, it is important to distinguish between their political disagreements and their relatively similar approaches to national security. Both prioritise military and security considerations, particularly regarding the Palestinians and Iran.”

An early test could come on Tuesday, when Eisenkot’s allies plan to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana of Likud with Yashar lawmaker Matan Kahana. Eisenkot has challenged Netanyahu and Smotrich to back Kahana and allow the vote to go ahead as scheduled, saying their response would show how serious they are about cooperation.

But even if Eisenkot and Netanyahu agreed on a policy plan for government, they still have to decide who leads. “The question of who would serve as prime minister remains the central obstacle,” Manna said. “Eisenkot has so far rejected a rotation arrangement with Netanyahu.”

Meanwhile, Netanyahu is still in office as caretaker prime minister while negotiations continue. That gives him an incentive to exploit divisions among Eisenkot’s potential partners and wait for his mandate to run out, experts say.

“At this stage, Netanyahu does not necessarily need to form a new coalition himself,” Manna said. “Preventing Eisenkot from forming one may be enough to preserve his position temporarily.”

Manna said Netanyahu could also use a security crisis to increase pressure for a national government. “A renewed large-scale confrontation could increase pressure for a national unity government or shift the priorities of coalition negotiations,” he said. “At the same time, it could generate new disagreements over military decision-making, the management of the conflict, and the authority of a caretaker government.”

If talks with the ultra-Orthodox parties fail, Levy said, Eisenkot could ask his allies to choose between accepting support from the Palestinian-led parties and leaving Netanyahu in office. He could also propose a short-lived government whose immediate purpose would be to replace Netanyahu and prepare for another election.

He added that in such a scenario, Eisenkot might tell his allies to “form a government for a few months, just to get Bibi [Netanyahu] out of power and prepare for new elections”.

This would prevent Netanyahu from using “his position as prime minister to create a crisis”.

“One of Eisenkot’s main difficulties is the opposition of Avigdor Lieberman and Naftali Bennett [leaders of parties in his alliance] to relying on Arab parties,” Yasser Manna, a researcher at the Jerusalem Center for Studies on Israeli Affairs, told Al Jazeera. “This position restricts Eisenkot’s coalition options, but it does not automatically make a unity government with Netanyahu more likely. Instead, it increases the importance of negotiations with other parties, particularly the ultra-Orthodox parties.”

The other main option, which according to experts is the most likely scenario, is the Eisenkot bloc going into a coalition with both ultra-Orthodox parties in Netanyahu’s bloc, Shas and United Torah Judaism, which would take the Eisenkot bloc to 61.

Advisers from one faction of United Torah Judaism have reportedly sought a written commitment from all 48 lawmakers in Eisenkot’s bloc to pass a law exempting Jewish religious seminary students from military service and to shield it from being struck down by the High Court. Eisenkot and Lieberman are reportedly opposed to this compromise.

President Herzog gave Eisenkot until December 6 to form a government. Herzog can grant an extension of up to 14 days, which would take the deadline to December 20.

Eisenkot has left the door open to members of Netanyahu’s Likud Party and to far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party, provided they back a government led by Eisenkot and accept his programme.

“If members of Likud and the Religious Zionist Party truly believe this is a time for unity, as they told the president, I cannot conceive of any reason why they would not support a government under my leadership and the principles I have presented,” Eisenkot said at the ceremony where Herzog handed him the mandate.

Daniel Levy, a former Israeli peace negotiator and president of the US/Middle East Project, told Al Jazeera that agreeing to meet can serve both men politically. “The coalition formation period is about spin and distortion and trying to gain leverage,” he told Al Jazeera. “So you take a meeting to show that you were willing to talk, then say the other side made unreasonable demands.”

The two men know each other well. Eisenkot led Israel’s military from 2015 to 2019 and served as an observer in Netanyahu’s war cabinet during the first eight months of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. He left the emergency government in June 2024.

“I believe the relationship between Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot is marked by a deep crisis of trust that goes beyond political competition,” Manna said. “However, it is important to distinguish between their political disagreements and their relatively similar approaches to national security. Both prioritise military and security considerations, particularly regarding the Palestinians and Iran.”

An early test could come on Tuesday, when Eisenkot’s allies plan to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana of Likud with Yashar lawmaker Matan Kahana. Eisenkot has challenged Netanyahu and Smotrich to back Kahana and allow the vote to go ahead as scheduled, saying their response would show how serious they are about cooperation.

But even if Eisenkot and Netanyahu agreed on a policy plan for government, they still have to decide who leads. “The question of who would serve as prime minister remains the central obstacle,” Manna said. “Eisenkot has so far rejected a rotation arrangement with Netanyahu.”

Meanwhile, Netanyahu is still in office as caretaker prime minister while negotiations continue. That gives him an incentive to exploit divisions among Eisenkot’s potential partners and wait for his mandate to run out, experts say.

“At this stage, Netanyahu does not necessarily need to form a new coalition himself,” Manna said. “Preventing Eisenkot from forming one may be enough to preserve his position temporarily.”

Manna said Netanyahu could also use a security crisis to increase pressure for a national government. “A renewed large-scale confrontation could increase pressure for a national unity government or shift the priorities of coalition negotiations,” he said. “At the same time, it could generate new disagreements over military decision-making, the management of the conflict, and the authority of a caretaker government.”

If talks with the ultra-Orthodox parties fail, Levy said, Eisenkot could ask his allies to choose between accepting support from the Palestinian-led parties and leaving Netanyahu in office. He could also propose a short-lived government whose immediate purpose would be to replace Netanyahu and prepare for another election.

He added that in such a scenario, Eisenkot might tell his allies to “form a government for a few months, just to get Bibi [Netanyahu] out of power and prepare for new elections”.

This would prevent Netanyahu from using “his position as prime minister to create a crisis”.

Who: Germany vs Netherlands
What: UEFA Nations League, Group A2
Where: Olympiastadion in Berlin, Germany

How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 16:45 GMT before our live text commentary stream.

Germany and the Netherlands head into the final Group A2 Nations League match hoping to secure their place in the quarterfinals.

Xavi Hernandez’s Netherlands side are practically through – barring a huge swing in goal difference – as they lead the table with 11 points after thrashing Greece 7-0 on Friday.

Jurgen Klopp’s Germany, who beat bottom placed Serbia 3-1 in their last game, know they will likely need a win to progress.

The Germans sit third with eight points, level with second-placed Greece but below them on their head-to-head record, which trumps goal difference as a tiebreaker in this season’s competition. Greece host Serbia, who have yet to win a point.

Germany cruised to a 3-1 win against Serbia in Belgrade on Friday.

The Germans forced Serbia’s Srdan Babic into an early own goal with Florian Wirtz and Brajan Gruda also scoring.

Babic made up for his blunder with a second-half consolation strike while Serbia finished with nine men after substitutes Vanja Dragojevic and Andrija Zivkovic were sent off late on.

Germany have now won twice, drawn twice and lost once in five games under Klopp.

Tijjani Reijnders netted a first-half hat-trick ⁠as the ⁠Netherlands thrashed Greece 7-0.

The Dutch ⁠were 5-0 up at the break with Crysencio Summerville putting the hosts ahead in the sixth minute before Reijnders ran riot and Jurrien ‌Timber notched their fifth before half-time.

Timber scored again just before the hour mark with Donyell Malen netting the final goal.

Klopp says his side are happy to have set up a deciding match against the Dutch.

“We wanted to set up a final against the Netherlands in Berlin, and now we have it,” Klopp said.

“We now have the chance to secure qualification for the next round in our own hands. We want to show everyone that German football is in good hands,” he said.

“We have good players, we’re working hard and we want to show in these matches that we’ve learned, that we’ve come together and that we’ve developed as a team. And that was definitely evident [against Serbia].

“The atmosphere in the camp is good, but that brings nothing if nobody can see it on the pitch. Our first job is to show the world that we can play football.”

The Opta supercomputer has made Germany the favourites with a win probability of 43.5 percent.

The Netherlands were given a 29.8 percent chance of winning while a draw was estimated at a 26.8 percent likelihood.

Cody Gakpo volleyed in a stoppage-time equaliser to rescue a 1-1 draw for the Netherlands against Germany in their Nations League Group A2 opener on September 24, denying Klopp a winning start to his tenure.

The visitors took a first-half lead with Felix Nmecha slotting in from close range. Karim Adeyemi should have scored another, but he somehow missed the target from 5 metres (5.5 yards) out.

The Dutch upped the pressure after the break and repeatedly came close to an equaliser with Germany’s new number one goalkeeper Marc-Andre ter Stegen making several good saves. But their dominance finally paid off with Gakpo’s late strike.

Bayern Munich stars Jamal Musiala and Serge Gnabry are unavailable due to muscle problems, but Germany have no other reported injury concerns.

Ter Stegen (goalkeeper); Treu, Thiaw, Tah, Mittelstadt; Kimmich, Pavlovic; Gruda, Wirtz, Scherhant; Havertz

Frenkie de Jong has returned to Barcelona for treatment after he went off with a back injury during the win over Greece. Teun Koopmeiners looks set to replace him in midfield.

Captain Virgil van Dijk did not join the squad during this international break due to injury, so Tottenham duo Micky van de Ven and Jan Paul van Hecke are likely to start as centre backs.

Verbruggen (goalkeeper); Dumfries, Van Hecke, Van de Ven, Timber; Veerman, Koopmeiners; Summerville, Reijnders, Gakpo; Malen

news.originalContent:
The remains of 69 Palestinians have been recovered in northern Gaza, allowing families to finally bury relatives they had spent years searching for.

Jabalia, Gaza Strip – Mahmoud Nabhan, a man in his sixties from Bir an-Naaja in northern Gaza, had waited more than three years for this day.

He wanted to give his loved ones a proper burial after 17 members of his family, including his seven children and grandchildren, were killed when their home was targeted 20 days after Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023. Among those killed was Nabhan’s 45-day-old grandchild.

After years of searching for their bodies, on Sunday Nabhan was finally able to bury his family members after Civil Defence teams retrieved their remains from the rubble of his home.

“All of them were children, all of them were loved ones,” he said.

Nabhan said there had been no fighters, Israeli soldiers or captives inside the home when it was struck.

For the past three years, he had tried to help recover his family’s remains, but the difficult conditions prevented this.

Their recovery from his destroyed home brought some relief for Nabhan, but it also brought more trauma.

“It feels as if they have just been killed again. The wounds have reopened,” he said. “But, thank God, we now know that our children have a grave here, beside their siblings, and we can visit them.”

The genocide in Gaza killed at least 73,600 people, with 82 per cent of the structures in Gaza damaged and two-thirds of them destroyed by waves of Israeli air strikes and shelling.

Under the rubble were thousands of bodies, with the continued attacks by Israeli forces often making it too dangerous for families or Civil Defence teams to retrieve them.

A truce agreed between Israel and Hamas in October 2025, which has been repeatedly broken by Israel, has allowed for some of the bodies to be recovered from the rubble that carpets Gaza

Civil Defence teams have managed to retrieve the remains of 69 Palestinians from locations in Jabalia refugee camp and Beit Lahiya in recent days.

For many families, the operation marked the end of years of uncertainty. Relatives had repeatedly followed up with Civil Defence, waiting for heavy machinery and other equipment to reach bodies trapped under collapsed buildings.

Fatima al-Masri, 47, said her husband and 18-year-old son were killed in an Israeli attack in the Safatwi area of northern Gaza in October 2024. Their remains have been buried beneath the rubble of their home for two years.

“Every month, every two months, sometimes every week or every two weeks, we would follow up with Civil Defence,” she said. “They told us they needed heavy equipment to lift the house because several floors had collapsed on top of them.”

After a long delay, the recovery operation began, with workers digging through the rubble using machines and by hand. They found bone fragments and al-Masri’s son’s mobile phone, along with the bodies and belongings of those who had been with her husband and son.

“Thank God, we found their remains and everything that was with them,” al-Masri said.

The two years of tortuous delays had left her in a constant state of anxiety. Every day, the same questions occupied her thoughts.

“I was always tense and worried. Every day, the same question was in my mind: ‘When would they recover them? When would we be able to bring them out?’” she said.

After the remains were recovered, she expressed relief that her husband and son could finally be buried.

The Palestinian Civil Defence estimates that more than 8,000 bodies are still to be recovered across Gaza.

The total number of missing Palestinians is estimated to exceed 10,000, although the broader figure includes people whose whereabouts remain unknown for different reasons, including those believed to be buried under rubble, detained or buried without identification.

Israel’s ongoing siege on Gaza means that Civil Defence teams have limited resources, with manual excavation often the only way to do their grim work.

According to Palestinian authorities cited by the United Nations, more than 630 bodies and human remains had been recovered from beneath destroyed buildings across Gaza since November 2025 by September 2026.

Ramiz Hassouna, a lecturer at Israa University, said the recovery of his brother’s remains, Montaser, brought nearly two years of uncertainty to an end.

He disappeared on November 8, 2024, during the Israeli military siege of Jabalia refugee camp. He was last known to be in the al-Faluja area, where he had been trapped with a group of friends.

For almost two years, the family received conflicting accounts about his fate. Some said he had been killed, while others believed he had been detained.

The uncertainty ended when Civil Defence teams recovered his remains from a destroyed building in al-Faluja and contacted the family.
He was identified through personal belongings, including his wristwatch, a miswak (a traditional teeth-cleaning stick) and a prayer booklet, as well as distinctive marks on his front teeth.

Hassouna could not bring himself to go and identify his brother’s remains, so asked his younger brother to go in his place.

“I personally could not bear to look at my brother in that condition. I left it to my younger brother to identify him,” he said.

The remains of the friends Montaser was with when he died were recovered together and buried in the same grave.

“As they accompanied one another in this life, they will accompany one another in the afterlife,” said Hassouna.

An investigative journalist’s home in Panama was attacked in a suspected bombing. He was away and his wife escaped unharmed. His newspaper La Prensa says he was preparing to publish an investigation implicating former officials and a government contractor.

news.originalContent:
Starlink has recently denied restricting internet speeds but Elon Musk suggested the US military could be behind it.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that speed restrictions by Starlink’s military-grade internet service had aided a wave of deadly Russian attacks across Ukraine.

Two people were killed on Saturday in a Russian drone attack on what Ukrainian officials called “critical infrastructure” in the northern Koriukivka region.

An energy facility was also hit in Odesa overnight on Sunday, leaving 41,000 households without electricity, Ukraine’s DTEK energy provider said in a Telegram statement.

Ukraine’s army said it shot down 106 of 132 Russian drones launched overnight.

Zelenskyy posted on X that Russia was targeting energy substations with Shahed drones, which both sides commonly attack each other with.

“And many of these strikes are getting through because restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there,” he posted, citing Starlink’s sister company and reiterating accusations that it was throttling internet speeds and hampering military operations.

The president said on Saturday that the internet restrictions had been in place for five days and that Starlink reported technical problems, but Ukraine does “not believe that is the case”.

It is the second such outage in recent weeks. Starlink, owned by US billionaire Elon Musk’s SpaceX, has denied restricting internet speeds. Last month, Musk said the United States government controls Starshield.

Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Sunday that it launched attacks targeting Ukraine’s military airfields, munitions depots and other military facilities.

Authorities also said that an electrical engineer was killed and four others were injured in Russia’s Taganrog region after Ukrainian drones attacked the area on Sunday.

Six people were injured in a drone attack in Nizhnekamsk, local officials said. The city, as well as the wider Trans-Kama region of Tatarstan, reported heavy Ukrainian attacks on industrial facilities and a residential building earlier on Sunday.

US negotiators concluded visits to both countries in recent days in attempts to secure a ceasefire, despite tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.

Zelenskyy said the US floated the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership.

Russia’s President Vladimir Putin is due to meet President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping in the Chinese city of Shenzhen this week – but Ukraine is not on the agenda. Analysts have compared the meeting to the Yalta conference of 1945, which saw the US, UK and former Soviet Union divide Germany and establish the United Nations.

However, in a statement on Sunday, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, dismissed Russia’s longstanding proposal to revise Europe’s security architecture.

“Putin is throwing around ideas about reshaping the European security order. In his dreams, he sees himself in Yalta in 1945. The problem is that to put forward ideas of this magnitude, you first need to win a world war,” he said.

“Putin is throwing around ideas about reshaping the European security order. In his dreams, he sees himself in Yalta in 1945. The problem is that to put forward ideas of this magnitude, you first need to win a world war,” he said.

news.title: ایتالیا شرکت متا را بابت دسترسی به عکس‌های کاربران  فیسبوک، بیش از ۸۰۰ میلیون یورو جریمه کرد
news.originalSummary:
ایتالیا، شرکت متا، غول شبکه‌های اجتماعی، را به‌دلیل دسترسی به عکس‌های کاربران اندروید بدون دریافت رضایت صریح آنها، ۸۰۵ میلیون یورو (معادل ۸۸۷ میلیون دلار) جریمه کرده‌ است.

سازمان حفاظت از داده‌های ایتالیا اعلام کرده است که متا به حدود ۲۰ میلیون کاربر تلفن‌های هوشمند اطلاع‌رسانی مناسبی نکرده بود که از طریق یکی از قابلیت‌های اپلیکیشن فیسبوک به عکس‌ها و ویدیوهایشان دسترسی دارد.

news.originalContent:
ایتالیا، شرکت متا، غول شبکه‌های اجتماعی، را به‌دلیل دسترسی به عکس‌های کاربران اندروید بدون دریافت رضایت صریح آنها، ۸۰۵ میلیون یورو (معادل ۸۸۷ میلیون دلار) جریمه کرده‌ است.

سازمان حفاظت از داده‌های ایتالیا اعلام کرده است که متا به حدود ۲۰ میلیون کاربر تلفن‌های هوشمند اطلاع‌رسانی مناسبی نکرده بود که از طریق یکی از قابلیت‌های اپلیکیشن فیسبوک به عکس‌ها و ویدیوهایشان دسترسی دارد.

این نهاد به متا دو ماه مهلت داده است تا این قابلیت را به‌طور پیش‌فرض غیرفعال کند و برای استفاده از آن، رضایت جداگانه کاربران را بگیرد.

این یکی از بزرگترین جریمه‌هایی است که تاکنون یک نهاد ایتالیایی علیه یک شرکت بزرگ فناوری اعمال کرده است.

موضوع این جریمه به قابلیتی مربوط می‌شود که عکس‌ها و ویدیوهای موجود در گالری تلفن همراه کاربران را به‌عنوان پیشنهادهایی برای انتشار پست در فیسبوک نمایش می‌دهد.

فیسبوک برای دسترسی به گالری عکس کاربران، فقط یک مجوز کلی در سطح اپلیکیشن درخواست می‌کرد.

به گفته نهاد ناظر ایتالیایی، اطلاعیه‌ای که پیش از آن به کاربران نمایش داده می‌شد، به‌روشنی توضیح نمی‌داد که این مجوز به فیسبوک اجازه می‌دهد بر اساس عکس‌های موجود در گالری تلفن همراه آنها هم پیشنهادهایی ارائه کند.

این نهاد اعلام کرد که در تعیین میزان جریمه، «تعداد زیاد افراد متأثر از این موضوع» و این واقعیت را در نظر گرفته است که این وضعیت «همچنان برای کاربرانی که اپلیکیشن خود را به‌روزرسانی نکرده‌اند و همچنین کسانی که پیشتر با این سازوکار موافقت کرده‌اند، ادامه دارد.»

نهاد ناظر ایتالیایی همچنین به «عدم همکاری متا» اشاره کرد. بی‌بی‌سی برای دریافت توضیحات در این باره با متا تماس گرفته است.

متا که همچون فیسبوک، شرکت مادر اینستاگرام و واتس‌اپ است ماه گذشته به‌دلیل شیوه‌های تجاری خود با بزرگترین جریمه تاریخ این شرکت روبه‌رو شد.

پس از آن که مشخص شد متا سال‌ها درباره نحوه مدیریت اطلاعات کاربران فیسبوک به افکار عمومی دروغ گفته، یک قاضی در ایالت نیومکزیکوی آمریکا این شرکت را به پرداخت ۲۵ میلیارد دلار  محکوم کرد.

news.originalTitle: بازگشت ناوشکن آمریکایی پس از ۳۵۷ روز ماموریت و شلیک ده‌ها موشک به ایران
news.title: بازگشت ناوشکن آمریکایی پس از ۳۵۷ روز ماموریت و شلیک ده‌ها موشک به ایران
news.originalSummary:
منبع تصویر، AFP via Getty Images

ناوشکن آمریکایی «یو‌اس‌اس اسپروئنس» که در جریان جنگ آمریکا و اسرائیل علیه ایران ده‌ها موشک کروز تاماهاک شلیک کرده بود، پس از ۳۵۷ روز ماموریت به پایگاه خود در سن‌دیگو در ایالت کالیفرنیا بازگشت. به گفته نیروی دریایی آمریکا، این طولانی‌ترین ماموریت یک ناوشکن این کشور از زمان جنگ جهانی دوم بوده است.

نیروی دریایی آمریکا روز جمعه ۱۳ نوامبر اعلام کرد که ناوشکن اسپروئنس

منبع تصویر، AFP via Getty Images

ناوشکن آمریکایی «یو‌اس‌اس اسپروئنس» که در جریان جنگ آمریکا و اسرائیل علیه ایران ده‌ها موشک کروز تاماهاک شلیک کرده بود، پس از ۳۵۷ روز ماموریت به پایگاه خود در سن‌دیگو در ایالت کالیفرنیا بازگشت. به گفته نیروی دریایی آمریکا، این طولانی‌ترین ماموریت یک ناوشکن این کشور از زمان جنگ جهانی دوم بوده است.

نیروی دریایی آمریکا روز جمعه ۱۳ نوامبر اعلام کرد که ناوشکن اسپروئنس
news.originalContent:
منبع تصویر، AFP via Getty Images

ناوشکن آمریکایی «یو‌اس‌اس اسپروئنس» که در جریان جنگ آمریکا و اسرائیل علیه ایران ده‌ها موشک کروز تاماهاک شلیک کرده بود، پس از ۳۵۷ روز ماموریت به پایگاه خود در سن‌دیگو در ایالت کالیفرنیا بازگشت. به گفته نیروی دریایی آمریکا، این طولانی‌ترین ماموریت یک ناوشکن این کشور از زمان جنگ جهانی دوم بوده است.

نیروی دریایی آمریکا روز جمعه ۱۳ نوامبر اعلام کرد که ناوشکن اسپروئنس پس از نزدیک به یک سال حضور در ماموریت‌های دریایی و نظامی، به پایگاه خود بازگشته است.

این ناوشکن ۲۱ نوامبر ۲۰۲۵، در قالب گروه رزمی ناو هواپیمابر «آبراهام لینکلن»، سن‌دیگو را ترک کرد. ماموریت آن ابتدا برای حدود هفت ماه برنامه‌ریزی شده بود، اما با آغاز جنگ علیه ایران تمدید شد و حتی پس از بازگشت ناو هواپیمابر آبراهام لینکلن، اسپروئنس در خاورمیانه باقی ماند.

به گفته نیروی دریایی آمریکا، این ناوشکن در طول ماموریت خود بیش از ۸۸ هزار مایل دریایی پیمود و در جریان جنگ با ایران، ده‌ها موشک تاماهاک به سوی اهداف نظامی شلیک کرد.

مقام‌های آمریکایی همچنین می‌گویند که اسپروئنس در جریان عملیات نظامی، ۱۲ پهپاد و چهار موشک کروز ضدکشتی را سرنگون کرده است.

ناوشکن اسپروئنس از جمله شناورهای آمریکایی بود که در نخستین روز جنگ، ۲۸ فوریه، در حملات موشکی به ایران مشارکت داشت.

در همان روز، مدرسه ابتدایی شجره طیبه در شهر میناب در استان هرمزگان هدف حمله قرار گرفت. به گفته مقام‌های ایرانی، بیش از ۱۷۵ نفر، از جمله شمار زیادی کودک، در این حمله کشته شدند.

خبرگزاری آسوشیتدپرس در ماه مارس گزارش داد که ناوشکن اسپروئنس در محدوده برد موشکی مدرسه میناب قرار داشت و فرماندهی مرکزی ارتش آمریکا، سنتکام، تصویری از شلیک موشک تاماهاک از این ناوشکن در روز ۲۸ فوریه منتشر کرده بود.

با این حال، هنوز مشخص نشده است که آیا موشک اصابت‌کرده به مدرسه میناب از همین ناوشکن شلیک شده بود یا نه.

بخش راستی‌آزمایی بی‌بی‌سی با بررسی تصاویر ویدئویی تایید کرد که یک موشک تاماهاک آمریکایی به مجموعه نظامی سپاه پاسداران در مجاورت مدرسه برخورد کرده است. بررسی‌های گروه تحقیقاتی بلینگکت نیز نشان داد که حملات به این مجموعه و مدرسه احتمالا در دست‌کم دو موج انجام شده بود.

رویترز پیش‌تر به نقل از مقام‌های آمریکایی گزارش داده بود که یافته‌های اولیه تحقیقات ارتش آمریکا از احتمال مسئولیت نیروهای این کشور در حمله به مدرسه حکایت دارد.

هیئت حقیقت‌یاب سازمان ملل متحد نیز در ماه سپتامبر اعلام کرد که دلایل معقولی برای انتساب حمله به مدرسه میناب به نیروهای آمریکایی وجود دارد و شواهد موجود می‌تواند نشان‌دهنده ارتکاب جنایت جنگی باشد.

مقام‌های آمریکایی یافته‌های این هیئت را رد کرده‌اند. گزارش نهایی تحقیقات وزارت دفاع آمریکا درباره حمله به مدرسه نیز به‌طور عمومی منتشر نشده است.

منبع تصویر، Corbis via Getty Images

ناوشکن اسپروئنس علاوه بر حملات موشکی به ایران، در عملیات دفاع در برابر پهپادها و موشک‌های ایرانی و همچنین محاصره دریایی بنادر ایران مشارکت داشت.

این ناوشکن در ماه آوریل یک کشتی باری ایرانی به نام «توسکا» را که به گفته سنتکام از دستور نیروهای آمریکایی برای توقف پیروی نکرده بود، هدف تیراندازی قرار داد.

ماموریت طولانی اسپروئنس در حالی پایان یافته است که ادامه استقرار ناوهای آمریکایی در خاورمیانه نگرانی‌هایی درباره فشار بر خدمه، فرسودگی تجهیزات و دشواری نگهداری از شناورهای جنگی ایجاد کرده است.

بازگشت این ناوشکن به سن‌دیگو، پایان یکی از طولانی‌ترین ماموریت‌های دریایی آمریکا در دهه‌های اخیر است؛ ماموریتی که بخش مهمی از آن با جنگ علیه ایران و عملیات نظامی در خاورمیانه همراه بود.

به گفته نیروی دریایی آمریکا، این ناوشکن در طول ماموریت خود بیش از ۸۸ هزار مایل دریایی پیمود و در جریان جنگ با ایران، ده‌ها موشک تاماهاک به سوی اهداف نظامی شلیک کرد.

مقام‌های آمریکایی همچنین می‌گویند که اسپروئنس در جریان عملیات نظامی، ۱۲ پهپاد و چهار موشک کروز ضدکشتی را سرنگون کرده است.

ناوشکن اسپروئنس از جمله شناورهای آمریکایی بود که در نخستین روز جنگ، ۲۸ فوریه، در حملات موشکی به ایران مشارکت داشت.

در همان روز، مدرسه ابتدایی شجره طیبه در شهر میناب در استان هرمزگان هدف حمله قرار گرفت. به گفته مقام‌های ایرانی، بیش از ۱۷۵ نفر، از جمله شمار زیادی کودک، در این حمله کشته شدند.

خبرگزاری آسوشیتدپرس در ماه مارس گزارش داد که ناوشکن اسپروئنس در محدوده برد موشکی مدرسه میناب قرار داشت و فرماندهی مرکزی ارتش آمریکا، سنتکام، تصویری از شلیک موشک تاماهاک از این ناوشکن در روز ۲۸ فوریه منتشر کرده بود.

با این حال، هنوز مشخص نشده است که آیا موشک اصابت‌کرده به مدرسه میناب از همین ناوشکن شلیک شده بود یا نه.

بخش راستی‌آزمایی بی‌بی‌سی با بررسی تصاویر ویدئویی تایید کرد که یک موشک تاماهاک آمریکایی به مجموعه نظامی سپاه پاسداران در مجاورت مدرسه برخورد کرده است. بررسی‌های گروه تحقیقاتی بلینگکت نیز نشان داد که حملات به این مجموعه و مدرسه احتمالا در دست‌کم دو موج انجام شده بود.

رویترز پیش‌تر به نقل از مقام‌های آمریکایی گزارش داده بود که یافته‌های اولیه تحقیقات ارتش آمریکا از احتمال مسئولیت نیروهای این کشور در حمله به مدرسه حکایت دارد.

هیئت حقیقت‌یاب سازمان ملل متحد نیز در ماه سپتامبر اعلام کرد که دلایل معقولی برای انتساب حمله به مدرسه میناب به نیروهای آمریکایی وجود دارد و شواهد موجود می‌تواند نشان‌دهنده ارتکاب جنایت جنگی باشد.

مقام‌های آمریکایی یافته‌های این هیئت را رد کرده‌اند. گزارش نهایی تحقیقات وزارت دفاع آمریکا درباره حمله به مدرسه نیز به‌طور عمومی منتشر نشده است.

منبع تصویر، Corbis via Getty Images

ناوشکن اسپروئنس علاوه بر حملات موشکی به ایران، در عملیات دفاع در برابر پهپادها و موشک‌های ایرانی و همچنین محاصره دریایی بنادر ایران مشارکت داشت.

این ناوشکن در ماه آوریل یک کشتی باری ایرانی به نام «توسکا» را که به گفته سنتکام از دستور نیروهای آمریکایی برای توقف پیروی نکرده بود، هدف تیراندازی قرار داد.

ماموریت طولانی اسپروئنس در حالی پایان یافته است که ادامه استقرار ناوهای آمریکایی در خاورمیانه نگرانی‌هایی درباره فشار بر خدمه، فرسودگی تجهیزات و دشواری نگهداری از شناورهای جنگی ایجاد کرده است.

بازگشت این ناوشکن به سن‌دیگو، پایان یکی از طولانی‌ترین ماموریت‌های دریایی آمریکا در دهه‌های اخیر است؛ ماموریتی که بخش مهمی از آن با جنگ علیه ایران و عملیات نظامی در خاورمیانه همراه بود.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

Apparently, 60 minutes of football wasn’t enough for Louisville and North Carolina on Saturday night.

The two ACC rivals decided to throw in a little extracurricular activity after the final whistle, turning an already heated contest into a full-blown postgame brawl.

Louisville escaped with a 16-14 victory over Bill Belichick’s Tar Heels, but the final score quickly became an afterthought when both sidelines emptied onto the field in a chaotic scene that looked more like a handful of heavyweight boxing matches than the conclusion of a college football game.

We got a brawl at the end of the Louisville vs UNC game pic.twitter.com/nIeyCwJuOc

The trouble began after North Carolina quarterback Travis Burgess threw a costly interception with just over a minute remaining, effectively ending the Tar Heels’ hopes of stealing a victory.

Louisville needed only to kneel down and run out the clock. Instead, the Cardinals’ final kneel-down became the opening bell for an all-out fight between the two teams.

Players began exchanging words before tempers boiled over, sending teammates pouring off both sidelines as pushing and shoving escalated into a sprawling melee.

Officials desperately blew their whistles and tossed penalty flags, although expecting a few yellow pieces of laundry to stop dozens of furious football players seemed about as effective as bringing a squirt gun to a burning building.

At one point, there were several skirmishes going on all over the field, including in the end zone.

For Belichick, the embarrassing spectacle added another ugly chapter to an already frustrating night.

North Carolina fell to 5-5 after letting a winnable game slip through its fingers, and now the Tar Heels must prepare for Virginia with questions surrounding both their execution and discipline.

The ACC could also have something to say about the confrontation if the conference decides additional punishment and suspensions are warranted.

news.originalContent:
Substitute Tatsuhiro Sakamoto’s late goal helps Japan avenge their defeat by Brazil in the World Cup round of 32.

Brazil forward Raphinha and manager Carlo Ancelotti were shown red cards for protesting against a referee’s decision in the South American giant’s shock defeat to Japan in a thrilling friendly match in Singapore.

Substitute Tatsuhiro Sakamoto netted his first international goal with a late winner on Saturday as Japan edged Brazil 3-2 at the National Stadium.

A brilliant brace by Vinicius Jr had erased a two-goal deficit after strikes by Takefusa Kubo and Keito Nakamura put the Samurai Blue 2-0 up in the opening 19 minutes.

But Sakamoto was in the right place to fire home after latching on to Kodai Sano’s deflected effort in stoppage time to give the Asian side a dramatic victory in front of 38,688 people.

Brazil appealed for a foul in the build-up to the goal, but VAR upheld the goal, and Raphinha and manager Ancelotti were shown red cards for their protests.

Ancelotti seemed surprised at the decision while Raphinha was led away by midfielder Marlon Gomes and team officials as he tried to approach referee Jansen Foo, who was instead confronted by Vinicius and Bruno Guimaraes.

“The referee gave me a red card because he said I wasn’t able to control the bench and that all the players were on the field,” Ancelotti said at a news conference.

“It’s a shame about the result because we don’t like to lose the game, but we have to look at what we did well. There are many positives. Some players who played for the first time showed good quality. For 70 minutes, the team played well.

“The result, obviously, was influenced by the referee’s performance, … but it’s not his fault. It was a high-level match, and I don’t think he had the experience to handle this kind of game.”

Raphinha was still fuming over the “unacceptable” red card as he critiqued the referee’s decisions while speaking to reporters after the match.

“First of all, I’d like to take this opportunity to apologise for my behaviour and for being sent off,” Raphinha said.

“Sometimes it’s hard to keep calm, especially after what I felt were so many refereeing errors during the match. I tried to speak to him several times, and not once did I feel he was open to discussion. I believe that he made many errors throughout the game, and that is unacceptable,” the Brazil captain said.

“In my view, their first goal involved a foul when the opponent took the ball off me with his hand. I think it’s a foul, but I can understand why it wasn’t given based on the current law. Then there was the penalty in the first half. In my opinion, it was a penalty, but he said no.

“Then, for their third goal, there was a clear foul on Joao Gomes. With the help of VAR, he eventually allowed the goal. It’s very difficult not to talk about the refereeing.”

The victory carried added significance for Japan, who suffered a heartbreaking exit to Brazil in the World Cup last 32 in June. On that occasion, Gabriel Martinelli struck in stoppage time to complete a 2-1 comeback win for the South Americans.

“I’m happy that I can say that today’s match was the best match in my eight-year tenure,” Japan head coach Hajime Moriyasu said after the game.

“Brazil’s intensity went up once we took the lead, and it was all about what we could do then.

“Our players performed at the world’s top standard. These wins lead to victories at the World Cup, and I hope they continue to do the same,” Moriyasu added.

The 58-year-old is expected to step down after a friendly against Paraguay on Tuesday and said he is looking forward to handing over to successor Go Oiwa.

“Now I need to pass the baton to the next coach, and that’s all I am focusing on.”

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Phil Collins gave a tearful acceptance speech and got an electrifying tribute from Cynthia Erivo, Oprah Winfrey inducted the late Luther Vandross, and Wu-Tang Clan made the Peacock Theater a rowdy celebration at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony on Saturday night.

Queen Latifah, Oasis, MC Lyte and Sade were also inducted, and Billy Idol, New Order and Iron Maiden were set to enter the hall later in the evening.

Collins, whose mobility issues and other health problems kept him from performing, took the stage slowly using a pair of canes and cried at a huge ovation from a crowd that included his daughter, actor Lily Collins.

Blink-182 drummer Travis Barker inducted Collins and praised him for his unprecedented dual stardom as a drummer and a hit-making pop singer in the 1980s.

“I grew up just wanting to play the drums,” Collins said. “Everything else has been a really happy accident. I can’t believe, when I look back, how life has gone.”

Barker said Collins’ song “In the Air Tonight” gave the world “arguably the most badass drum fill of all time.”

Minutes later, Barker played that fill himself as Erivo gave a slowed-down, epic rendition of the song that brought the crowd to its feet.

Collins was already in the hall as a member of Genesis, but now gets the solo honor.

He hasn’t been able to take the stage since 2022, but assured the crowd that “you haven’t heard the last of me.”

Winfrey, whose presence was unannounced, said with relish that Vandross was “the maestro of the love song” and said he was once correctly named “the top artist that people make looove to.”

Vandross, an R&B singer with a velvet voice, was one of the definitive singers of the 1980s and ’90s. He died in 2005.

“Luther Vandross sang with such passion and soul it could reach something deep inside that you didn’t even know needed to be reached,” Winfrey said.

Usher then took the stage and sang a sultry medley of Vandross hits, including “Here and Now” and “So Amazing.”

Wu-Tang Clan, the epic hip-hop collective from New York’s Staten Island, filled the stage with its 10 current members, giving a memorable acceptance speech and a performance that had the crowd on its feet and dancing.

Backed by a big jazz band, the musical medley included “C.R.E.A.M.,” “Method Man” and late member Ol’ Dirty Bastard’s “Shimmy Shimmy Ya.”

“Wu-Tang rewrote the rules of hip-hop and did it without a big machine behind them,” said comedian Chris Rock, who inducted them.

“We took Staten Island to the world,” the group’s leader RZA said. “We had a desire to conquer.”

He added, “We wanted to make a mark. We made our mark.”

MC Lyte, a trailblazing female rapper starting in the late 1980s, was the first artist inducted, with hip-hop star Remy Ma doing the honors and calling her “one of the first women in hip-hop to make sure there was room for the rest of us.”

MC Lyte said she was a “B-girl from Brooklyn just looking for my chance to inspire and motivate.” She did not perform at the moment of her induction but may be part of an ensemble later in the evening.

Her contemporary and fellow groundbreaker Latifah was inducted later in the evening by Megan Thee Stallion, who said Latifah “taught us to recognize royalty within ourselves.”

Latifah wore a leather crown that matched her leather trenchcoat and tie. She said, for a long time, she would not have believed this night was possible.

“It’s difficult enough being a woman in hip-hop, let alone being a hip-hopper in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame,” she said.

Latifah and MC Lyte then took the stage together to perform a medley of their hits, including Latifah’s “U.N.I.T.Y.” and Lyte’s “Ruffneck,” as members of Wu-Tang and Chuck D of Public Enemy danced and rapped along in the audience.

Latifah and Lyte entered the hall as recipients of the Early Influence Award along with posthumous nominees Gram Parsons, Fela Kuti and Celia Cruz.

U2 was the night’s surprise opener, playing their new single “Silencio” while surrounded by dancers in riot squad gear with helmets and shields. They then launched into their 1984 classic “Pride (In the Name of Love).”

Singer Bono alternately raised a peace sign and fist as guitarist the Edge and the rest of the band played the song about Martin Luther King, Jr. on the stage at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. U2 was inducted into the hall in 2005.

Oasis, the youngest of the inductees, didn’t show up. Guitarist Noel Gallagher is playing a gig back home in Britain, and his little brother, Liam Gallagher, just didn’t want to come.

“Anybody surprised they didn’t show up?” asked actor and Oasis superfan Bob Odenkirk, who inducted them. ”It would’ve been out of character if they had. I would’ve been worried about them.”

He praised their “bangers that make you sing along even before you finish hearing them for the first time,” before singer-songwriter Stephen Wilson Jr. gave an acoustic rendition of “Wonderwall.”

Sade also decided to skip the induction. The singer and her band that’s named after her were inducted by singer Andra Day and celebrated by singer Sienna Spiro, who sang the group’s beloved hit “Smooth Operator.”

Iron Maiden, to be inducted later Saturday night, was on tour in Australia. Key members of New Order, getting a joint induction with their previous incarnation Joy Division, will also be out for health reasons.

Phil Collins gave a tearful acceptance speech and got an electrifying tribute from Cynthia Erivo, Oprah Winfrey inducted the late Luther Vandross, and Wu-Tang Clan made the Peacock Theater a rowdy celebration at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony on Saturday night.

Queen Latifah, Oasis, MC Lyte and Sade were also inducted, and Billy Idol, New Order and Iron Maiden were set to enter the hall later in the evening.

Collins, whose mobility issues and other health problems kept him from performing, took the stage slowly using a pair of canes and cried at a huge ovation from a crowd that included his daughter, actor Lily Collins.

Blink-182 drummer Travis Barker inducted Collins and praised him for his unprecedented dual stardom as a drummer and a hit-making pop singer in the 1980s.

“I grew up just wanting to play the drums,” Collins said. “Everything else has been a really happy accident. I can’t believe, when I look back, how life has gone.”

Barker said Collins’ song “In the Air Tonight” gave the world “arguably the most badass drum fill of all time.”

Minutes later, Barker played that fill himself as Erivo gave a slowed-down, epic rendition of the song that brought the crowd to its feet.

Collins was already in the hall as a member of Genesis, but now gets the solo honor.

He hasn’t been able to take the stage since 2022, but assured the crowd that “you haven’t heard the last of me.”

Winfrey, whose presence was unannounced, said with relish that Vandross was “the maestro of the love song” and said he was once correctly named “the top artist that people make looove to.”

Vandross, an R&B singer with a velvet voice, was one of the definitive singers of the 1980s and ’90s. He died in 2005.

“Luther Vandross sang with such passion and soul it could reach something deep inside that you didn’t even know needed to be reached,” Winfrey said.

Usher then took the stage and sang a sultry medley of Vandross hits, including “Here and Now” and “So Amazing.”

Wu-Tang Clan, the epic hip-hop collective from New York’s Staten Island, filled the stage with its 10 current members, giving a memorable acceptance speech and a performance that had the crowd on its feet and dancing.

Backed by a big jazz band, the musical medley included “C.R.E.A.M.,” “Method Man” and late member Ol’ Dirty Bastard’s “Shimmy Shimmy Ya.”

“Wu-Tang rewrote the rules of hip-hop and did it without a big machine behind them,” said comedian Chris Rock, who inducted them.

“We took Staten Island to the world,” the group’s leader RZA said. “We had a desire to conquer.”

He added, “We wanted to make a mark. We made our mark.”

MC Lyte, a trailblazing female rapper starting in the late 1980s, was the first artist inducted, with hip-hop star Remy Ma doing the honors and calling her “one of the first women in hip-hop to make sure there was room for the rest of us.”

MC Lyte said she was a “B-girl from Brooklyn just looking for my chance to inspire and motivate.” She did not perform at the moment of her induction but may be part of an ensemble later in the evening.

Her contemporary and fellow groundbreaker Latifah was inducted later in the evening by Megan Thee Stallion, who said Latifah “taught us to recognize royalty within ourselves.”

Latifah wore a leather crown that matched her leather trenchcoat and tie. She said, for a long time, she would not have believed this night was possible.

“It’s difficult enough being a woman in hip-hop, let alone being a hip-hopper in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame,” she said.

Latifah and MC Lyte then took the stage together to perform a medley of their hits, including Latifah’s “U.N.I.T.Y.” and Lyte’s “Ruffneck,” as members of Wu-Tang and Chuck D of Public Enemy danced and rapped along in the audience.

MEMPHIS, Tenn. — The Nets had to play without their leading scorer Saturday, as Michael Porter Jr. sat on the bench in street clothes.

He watched his team take a 129-110 beating in Memphis at FedExForum.

Porter wasn’t injured but was a healthy scratch for personal reasons.

Two sources — one a team source and another close to the player — said the issue was believed to be resolved and Porter shouldn’t miss extended time.

When asked if he had a timeline for Porter’s return, Nets coach Jordi Fernández said, “No. We want to give him his privacy. Everything is fine, so we’re happy that he was here.”

Initially listed as questionable, Porter was ruled out an hour before tipoff.

“A personal situation came up as we were coming to the arena. So that’s why it was announced late,” Fernández said.

Porter is averaging a team-high 21.5 points on 45.6 percent shooting and 37.5 percent from deep. An Eastern Conference scout who spoke with The Post pointed out how easy the Nets are to defend without his unblockable shot. Julius Randle — Brooklyn’s other proven veteran scorer — said others simply have to pick up the slack.

“Everybody has to step in and chip in. It’s not just one person,” Randle said. “So we’ve all got to step up and chip in and do it collectively as a unit.”

Day’Ron Sharpe (16 points, 11 rebounds, five assists) had his third double-double of the season already. His career high is six in 2023-24.

Fernández handed Noah Clowney the start at small forward for Porter. With Randle, Sharpe, Egor Dëmin and Danny Wolf, every Nets starter was at least 6-foot-9 or taller, just as they had been in the blowout win in New Orleans three nights earlier.

This was the first time any NBA team had started a lineup of players all 6-foot-9 or taller since the Los Angeles Lakers had done so April 21, 1990.

Mikel Brown Jr. and Nolan Traore both returned after having missed the blowout win in New Orleans three nights earlier. It marked just the third game that the Nets have had Dëmin, Brown and Traore together.

Fernández said Brown is still on his minutes limit. With Wolf still starting at two-guard, Brown and Traore logged just 19 minutes each.

The Nets got thrown into travel chaos Friday by the Federal Aviation Administration’s decision to ground every flight nationwide for four hours. They were already set to board their flight but had to stay overnight in New Orleans and fly to Memphis at 9 a.m.

“Yeah, obviously it was something that we couldn’t control,” Fernández said. “And to be honest with you, it was not that bad. We had good rest and got here [Saturday] morning and did our walk-through, and probably [would have] gone to the gym, but we were not able to. And I think we feel good and ready to go.”

ANAHEIM, Calif. — The Islanders had Mathew Barzal back for Saturday’s match against the Ducks but operated with caution regarding immediate expectations for him.

“Obviously he’s gotta transition back into full speed,” coach Pete DeBoer said before the 6-2 win. “We’re gonna work him into that, but it’s great that he’s available to play.”

What that means on a practical level is the Islanders will manage Barzal’s ice time closely — including 16:21 on Saturday. He’ll also start on the second power-play unit as opposed to the top group.

Jean-Gabriel Pageau missed a second straight game with a lower-body injury, and Calum Ritchie remains out with a lower-body injury, so there’s still some suspense over what the lineup will look like when fully healthy. Saturday, though, Barzal skated in Pageau’s usual spot on the third line between Ondrej Palat and Anthony Duclair, with no changes to the Islanders top six.

Matthew Kessel, who played as the seventh defenseman against the Kings two nights prior, was the healthy scratch, with the Islanders going back to a 12-forward, six-defenseman configuration.

“I’m not sure [what to expect], honestly, it’s been a while,” Barzal said. “So obviously I’m just excited. I know how I am. I know that when I get out there, I’m gonna want to play. I’m gonna want to be going over the boards a ton. We gotta be controlled, and the team’s been playing well. Just trying to hop in, bring what I bring. I know as soon as I hit that ice, I’m gonna want to go.”

DeBoer declined to commit to a number for Barzal’s minutes when asked, but it did seem clear that the 20:39 he averaged a year ago wasn’t going to be in the cards right away.

“He’s getting back in, he’s playing his first game in six or seven months,” DeBoer said. “We’re gonna manage his ice time, and we know there’s gonna be some runway here where he’s gotta work himself back into game shape and game timing. But it’s gonna be a great first step.”

Kyle MacLean was put on non-roster waivers to make room for Barzal. If he clears, he’ll likely be sent down to AHL Hamilton.

“That’s a tough conversation. Great pro, great kid, great man,” DeBoer said. “… He’s been a great, great Islander here. Been a lot of heavy lifting and work for a long time, so those are always tough.”

Ritchie (lower body) has started to skate on his own back in New York.

Logan Stanley left the game with a lower-body injury early in the second period and did not return. DeBoer said he would be evaluated Sunday upon the team’s return to New York.

news.originalContent:
Energy disruptions as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran is a key issue for the import-dependent bloc.

Southeast Asian countries that comprise the ASEAN economic bloc will meet in the Philippines this week as the region continues to bear the brunt of oil shortages caused by the US-Israel war on Iran, as well as by US-China rivalry, which has hit economies hard.

The Manila summit will be held from November 15 to 17 and will include US President Donald Trump and several other world leaders.

The 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) aims to establish a single market, although it cannot impose decisions on members. It comprises Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Brunei, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar, Cambodia and East Timor, with a combined population of nearly 694 million, or 8.4 percent of the world’s population.

Several ASEAN meetings are held annually. This week’s summit is expected to be the final one for this year.

Beyond the energy crisis, other pressing issues include disputes over the South China Sea and trade.

In addition to leaders and representatives from the 11 member countries, other guests include:

The summit is being held at a time when Southeast Asian countries have been hit hard by shortages in oil and gas supplies from Middle Eastern suppliers amid the US-Israel war on Iran.

The Philippines, Vietnam and Malaysia are among the most vulnerable to the energy disruptions in the Gulf, with Manila declaring a state of national energy emergency in March.

Millions of ASEAN citizens also live and work in the Middle East, where the war threatens their safety and earnings.

Meanwhile, Asian countries are worried the conflict could spill into the Strait of Malacca, a narrow waterway between Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore.

The US’s tariff war has seen ASEAN countries slapped with 10-12.5 percent tariff hikes since the beginning of US President Donald Trump’s second term in the White House, prompting the bloc to strengthen trade relationships elsewhere.

China and four ASEAN members – Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam – as well as Taiwan, have been locked in decades of territorial standoffs in the busy waterway.

The area is important as it is believed to host undersea deposits of oil and gas.

In 2005, the bloc began negotiating a “code of conduct” with China to discourage aggression and prevent major clashes. The negotiations have often stalled, however, partly due to flared tensions, especially between Manila and Beijing in recent years.

In 2023, the two sides agreed to speed things up and release a finished draft this year. At least 10 rounds of talks have been held this year, led by Malaysia, with a final round taking place in October.

However, analysts doubt a definite conclusion will be reached at the summit this week, meaning talks could continue into next year.

Armed clashes broke out between the two ASEAN member states late last year along an 800km (500-mile) contested border area, as well as over competing claims to sacred religious sites, such as the Preah Vihear Shiva temple.

At least 150 people were reported to have been killed, and nearly one million displaced.

ASEAN members, as well as China and the US, intervened, leading to talks. Although a ceasefire has been in place since December, the wider border dispute remains unresolved, and the bloc is calling for more dialogue and the participation of third-party observers.

The ongoing civil war in Myanmar, which has compounded the Rohingya refugee crisis, has been at the top of the agenda as the bloc pushes for the restoration of democracy in the country.

Multiple rebel forces, some of them ethnic-based armed groups, have been fighting the military government since the country’s February 2021 coup.

ASEAN has already restricted Myanmar’s participation at important summits to non-political representatives as concerns about violence and a humanitarian crisis grow.

The bloc’s five-point Myanmar peace plan, launched in April 2021 and calling for dialogue and improved humanitarian aid access, has meanwhile failed to alleviate the situation.

Months of widespread wildfires in drought-hit Indonesia have scorched an estimated 2.88 million hectares (7.12 million acres) and resulted in at least 3,500 deaths.

The resulting haze has severely impacted not just the country’s residents, but also those in neighbouring Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and East Timor.

Jakarta has faced criticism for failing to effectively respond to the fires, but the government has defended its approach, saying thousands of responders have been deployed.

The summit is being held at a time when Southeast Asian countries have been hit hard by shortages in oil and gas supplies from Middle Eastern suppliers amid the US-Israel war on Iran.

The Philippines, Vietnam and Malaysia are among the most vulnerable to the energy disruptions in the Gulf, with Manila declaring a state of national energy emergency in March.

Millions of ASEAN citizens also live and work in the Middle East, where the war threatens their safety and earnings.

Meanwhile, Asian countries are worried the conflict could spill into the Strait of Malacca, a narrow waterway between Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore.

The US’s tariff war has seen ASEAN countries slapped with 10-12.5 percent tariff hikes since the beginning of US President Donald Trump’s second term in the White House, prompting the bloc to strengthen trade relationships elsewhere.

China and four ASEAN members – Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam – as well as Taiwan, have been locked in decades of territorial standoffs in the busy waterway.

The area is important as it is believed to host undersea deposits of oil and gas.

In 2005, the bloc began negotiating a “code of conduct” with China to discourage aggression and prevent major clashes. The negotiations have often stalled, however, partly due to flared tensions, especially between Manila and Beijing in recent years.

In 2023, the two sides agreed to speed things up and release a finished draft this year. At least 10 rounds of talks have been held this year, led by Malaysia, with a final round taking place in October.

However, analysts doubt a definite conclusion will be reached at the summit this week, meaning talks could continue into next year.

Armed clashes broke out between the two ASEAN member states late last year along an 800km (500-mile) contested border area, as well as over competing claims to sacred religious sites, such as the Preah Vihear Shiva temple.

At least 150 people were reported to have been killed, and nearly one million displaced.

ASEAN members, as well as China and the US, intervened, leading to talks. Although a ceasefire has been in place since December, the wider border dispute remains unresolved, and the bloc is calling for more dialogue and the participation of third-party observers.

The ongoing civil war in Myanmar, which has compounded the Rohingya refugee crisis, has been at the top of the agenda as the bloc pushes for the restoration of democracy in the country.

Multiple rebel forces, some of them ethnic-based armed groups, have been fighting the military government since the country’s February 2021 coup.

ASEAN has already restricted Myanmar’s participation at important summits to non-political representatives as concerns about violence and a humanitarian crisis grow.

The bloc’s five-point Myanmar peace plan, launched in April 2021 and calling for dialogue and improved humanitarian aid access, has meanwhile failed to alleviate the situation.

Months of widespread wildfires in drought-hit Indonesia have scorched an estimated 2.88 million hectares (7.12 million acres) and resulted in at least 3,500 deaths.

The resulting haze has severely impacted not just the country’s residents, but also those in neighbouring Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and East Timor.

Jakarta has faced criticism for failing to effectively respond to the fires, but the government has defended its approach, saying thousands of responders have been deployed.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

There was no joy at Madison Square Garden by the end of the night, only vocal displeasure with who was deemed the winner of the UFC 334 heavyweight title fight.

The fans wanted Josh Hokit to take the belt off Ciryl Gane on Saturday night (which bled into Sunday). The three judges had other ideas, awarding unanimous 48-47 scorecards.

“I will rejoice in my suffering. Suffering builds endurance. And endurance builds hope,” said Hokit afterward in the Octagon, absent his typical ugly brashness on the mic in the wake of his first career loss.

Hokit, an overwhelming darling of the Garden crowd, immediately shot for and secured a single-leg takedown, but Gane managed to get back to striking distance. Hokit’s frantic pressure made the Muay Thai striker from France less comfortable than normal but still more successful in landing punches against the brawling American, though Hokit in turn found his successes.

Gane again got snatched up for a more thunderous takedown late in the first frame, this time atop the center logo, and Hokit added some strikes for good measure to end a competitive opening round.

Hokit shot again to start the second, but Gane was finally ready for it and deftly defended. The uppercut, a solid weapon in the first, was again landing for Gane, and followed up in combination as Hokit’s frenetic energy settled.

But Gane noticeably had slowed by the midway point as well, and Hokit continued to walk forward. Wild punches from Hokit found a home with increasing regularity on the Frenchman, whose face bore a small smear of blood from his nose. They appeared to be getting to him.

Tired as he appeared, Gane fared better at stuffing takedowns, or at least not going down for long, early in the third. Instead, Hokit switched to clinch work and dirty boxing to find success on offense. He force-fed flips of the bird to cap off the frame, a staple of his public persona. Gane was not without his own damage dealt in the frame, however.

Gane, finding a second wind but clearly not up on the scorecards, mixed in some big knees early in the fourth, but little deterred Hokit from coming forward on this night. Clinch work once again was Hokit’s bread and butter, though Gane was more active in establishing enough high-impact offense to perhaps top Hokit’s output.

The final round began as most had before, with a Hokit takedown attempt. Gane defended, and a phone-booth boxing match ensued. The technique of Gane helped him find more accurate lands early on than the more wild ex-football player. But the fifth round was as competitive as the last two, and the offense hardly relented before the final horn before awaiting the official decision.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Comedian Bill Maher issued a preemptive warning to Democrats after their sweeping midterm election wins, urging the party not to mistake its victories for a mandate to revive “bad ideas” that could drive voters back to the GOP.

“Now that Democrats won the election, let’s not get high on our own supply like the last crowd did and interpret the W as a sign to go back to bad ideas,” he said during Friday’s episode of “Real Time.”

The liberal comedian pointed to “defund the police” and a refusal to enforce shoplifting laws, arguing that such approaches hurt the people progressives claim to help.

Maher also mocked progressives he described as the “lawn sign people,” accusing them of using yard signs touting equality, science and kindness to advertise their moral superiority.

“It’s all well and good to declare yourself the morally enlightened ones, but when your policy ideas are based on how good they make you feel and not on how much good they actually do, that’s when people lurch to the other even worse extreme,” he said.

Criticizing policies in Democratic-led cities, Maher asked, “Who benefited when you didn’t enforce the laws against shoplifting? Who benefits when you give a homeless schizophrenic clean needles instead of forcing him into treatment?”

Maher also criticized what he characterized as white liberals’ approach to racial issues, joking, “I talked to every black person in America, and it turns out they kind of don’t give a s—. Yeah. Turns out they’re not waking up every day saying, ‘What can I do today to make sure white people feel better about themselves?’”

Tim Graham, the executive editor of the Media Research Center’s NewsBusters blog, told Fox News Digital, “None of the elitist media are anywhere near the kind of tough-love advice counselor for Democrats, and especially not in public. If they wanted to tell Democrats that their gooey intentions aren’t equivalent to outcomes, they’d do it off the record.”

Christian Toto, the editor of Hollywood in Toto, told Fox News Digital, “Bill Maher is the most refreshing, unexpected pundit on late-night TV. He calls balls and strikes while simultaneously copping to his liberal bona fides.”

Toto added that Maher is “a pariah of sorts within his industry” and predicted that the “modern left will happily ignore his wisdom, likely at their political peril.”

Jason Mudd, CEO of Axia Public Relations, told Fox News Digital, “If the Democratic Party were my client, I’d advise them to remember this win was more about Trump than about the party.

“They should lean moderate to win over more voters. I’d also have trusted advisors with an objective or contrarian view screen each message before it goes public.”

Maher also criticized conservatives, arguing that Democrats won across several states in the midterms because voters have a history of shifting from one political extreme to another.

He first rejected what he characterized as Democratic moral superiority, then criticized what he described as Republicans’ embrace of “cruelty.”

“Republicans lost this election because no one wanted the pendulum to swing all the way to full a–hole, to cruelty,” he said.

“Yes, liberal virtue signaling had become tiresome, but did we have to go to vice signaling?”

Maher pointed to fatal shootings during immigration enforcement, cuts to the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) and other incidents as examples of what he believed caused the political pendulum to swing back to the left.

“This is how you lose even Texas,” he insisted, referring to wins for Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa in the longtime red stronghold.

“Everything is a reaction to what went before,” he added later.

Maher made the comments as Republicans review their midterm losses and reassess the party’s strategy ahead of the 2028 elections.

Republican candidates were upset in a handful of red and purple states, including South Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Mississippi and Georgia earlier this month, leading to Democratic majorities in both houses of Congress.

news.originalContent:
For all its green-washing, the Zionist state has ecologically devastated Palestine more than anyone else.

A Palestinian writer from Gaza.

A month into this year’s olive harvest season, Israeli settlers and soldiers have already damaged or uprooted 4,500 olive trees in the occupied West Bank. Since January, they have destroyed 100,000 olive trees. In Gaza, since October 2023, 97 percent of Gaza’s two million olive oil trees have been wiped out. Between 1967, when Israel occupied Gaza and the West Bank, and the 2010s, it had destroyed more than 800,000.

I think of the devastating sight of uprooted trees in my grandfather’s olive grove every time I hear news of Israel sending yet another delegation to a climate, biodiversity, or desertification conference to boast of its “unique expertise” in “making the desert bloom” – a myth it has long propagated.

The destruction of olive trees is just one aspect of Israel’s broader war on the Palestinian land, from its vegetation and soil to its water and ecosystems. Since the Nakba of 1948, Israeli colonial policies have extended beyond land seizure and the displacement of its inhabitants to reshaping the natural landscape, undermining its capacity to sustain those who have lived on and cultivated it for generations.

In other words, contrary to its greenwashing claims, Israel made a blooming Palestine burn.

When the first Zionist settlers started coming to Palestine in the late 19th century, what they found was “a desert” that was already blooming. Palestinian land was producing not only enough food to feed its people but also to export to neighbouring regions within the Ottoman Empire and even across the Mediterranean to Europe.

Palestinians were growing wheat, barley and oats and harvesting olive and fruit trees. Closer to the Mediterranean coast, lush gardens produced various vegetables and fruit. In the more arid Naqab desert in the south, Bedouin tribes tended to herds of sheep, goats and camels, producing meat, milk and wool.

Palestinians co-existed with the various ecosystems they occupied: from wetlands to the dry desert. They tended to the land using techniques that reflected local conditions rather than seeking to engineer them. Local drought-resistant crops were grown in drier areas and more irrigation-dependent ones in valleys closer to water sources.

By contrast, Zionist settlers coming from Europe sought to reshape Palestine’s landscape to what was familiar to them. They planted trees imported from Europe, such as the stone pine, in some cases uprooting native species, including olive trees. They drained swamps, rerouted streams and tried to afforest desert landscapes.

Some of these activities had disastrous consequences for local ecosystems, including the introduction of non-native plants such as the eucalyptus, which burns easily and which has contributed to a higher frequency and intensity of wildfires.

Israel’s efforts to reshape the natural landscape were driven by the desire to erase Palestinian presence. Trees were planted over the remains of pillaged Palestinian villages to cover them up. Imported European-style agriculture wiped out native Palestinian techniques that had produced food for centuries.

The Zionist assault on the Palestinian land did not stop at the 1948 boundaries. As soon as the Israeli army occupied the West Bank and Gaza, it put under martial rule not just the people but also their natural resources.

Water has been at the centre of this process. As illegal settlements spread in the occupied territories, settlers started taking over local water resources. Today, Israel’s national water company, Mekorot, is responsible for running an extensive water system that reroutes water from Palestinian towns and villages to the Israeli settlements. It often cuts off water to Palestinians in the summer to ensure a steady supply to the illegal settlers.

This water theft has devastated Palestinian agriculture and ecosystems.

Meanwhile, land theft has featured not only violence against the Palestinian people but also against their soil. For years, the Israeli army and settlers have sprayed Palestinian land with pesticides to discourage farmers from working their fields. Meanwhile, burning and uprooting of trees and other vegetation, as well as settler construction, have damaged the soil and led to erosion.

In Gaza, ecocide has been taken to the extreme. The genocidal war unleashed on the Gaza Strip has devastated agricultural land, trees, soil and water.

These harms are compounded by bombardment and bulldozing. Israel has destroyed approximately 85 percent of buildings in the Gaza Strip, leaving an estimated 70 million tonnes of rubble containing various toxins. Israeli bombardment has dispersed heavy metals, including lead, cadmium, arsenic, tungsten and aluminium, as well as explosive compounds such as TNT, RDX and perchlorates.

These substances seep into the soil and groundwater, causing environmental damage whose effects may persist for years.

Meanwhile, the continuing bulldozing of buildings and land has stripped away the topsoil, which is rich in organic matter and nutrients essential for plant growth, further degrading agricultural land.

The paradox here is that the Israelis who claim to have an ancient right to the land are the very same people who damage and destroy it. This is highly surprising.

A coloniser sees land as something to capture, possess and exploit. The colonial relationship to land is one of abuse for the sake of material benefit. It is not care. It is not stewardship. It is not belonging.

The Israeli approach to Palestinian land – poison and destroy in order to control – contrasts sharply with the Palestinian one. Since 1948, Palestinians have faced constant attacks, destruction, theft of resources, pillaging. And yet, they have sought to rebuild, replant and rework over and over again.

My own grandfather, Hamdan, is an example of this Palestinian spirit. For four decades he looked over an eight-dunam olive grove that produced 1,500kg of olive oil each season.

During the 2008 war, the Israeli army bulldozed the grove. My grandfather did not relent. He replanted olive trees with my help. Just as the grove was beginning to recover, the Israeli army destroyed it again during the 2014 war.

For my grandfather, the olive trees were more than a livelihood. He saw them as his children, the fruit of years of care and his family’s bond to the land. Less than a week after their destruction in 2014, my grandfather died from the shock.

We did not relent either. My family set out to restore and replant the land with olive trees in 2015, which took several months. The trees then took three years to bear fruit. We managed to harvest olives for two seasons before the Israeli army bombed the grove during the 2021 war.

The land was so damaged that it was no longer suitable for olive cultivation. Clearing the contamination and burying the bomb craters took a long time, but we still managed to plant some of the land with seasonal crops like wheat. Then in December 2023, the Israeli army devastated the grove again.

I would be replanting that land again today if it didn’t lie beyond the ever-expanding “Yellow Line”.

That drive to tend to land is so deeply ingrained in Palestinians that even in the camps for the displaced, people are keeping small gardens in front of their tents, planting mint, basil and flowers.

Despite all the propaganda and greenwashing Israel deploys, it is increasingly clear to the world who can make the Holy Land bloom. It is not those who destroy, poison and bulldoze. It is those who are deeply rooted, who plant, grow and care. Those are the true owners of the land.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

news.title: The French Republic’s forgotten promise of equality
