The US has floated the possibility of Ukraine joining NATO in exchange for surrendering its remaining territory in the war-ravaged Donbas region to Russia, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

“The Americans raised the question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’ This was the first time this issue had been raised,” Zelensky told reporters Friday, in comments released Saturday.

Russia controls about 80% of Donetsk and nearly all of Luhansk, the two mineral-rich eastern Ukrainian provinces that make up the Donbas, according to Nov. 11 estimates by the US-based Institute for the Study of War.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has long demanded that Ukraine pull out of the Donbas region entirely as a condition for a cease-fire.

Zelensky said he would put any proposed deal to the Ukrainian people if Washington and its NATO allies spell out a comprehensive security package that includes weapons, postwar recovery assistance and funding.

“If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not? I have no right to make that decision on my own,” Zelensky said.

“We need specifics, and we don’t have them yet. All of this is still under discussion.”

The Ukrainian leader insisted, however, that any agreement would come “without any recognition of the occupied territories as Russian,” according to the Kyiv Independent.

He’s long held the position that he could only accept freezing the war along the current front line, which would see Ukraine retain 20% of Donetsk.

Meanwhile, the US, Ukraine and Russia have agreed to bring as many as five European representatives directly into peace negotiations following trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi this week.

European leaders have worried that the US-brokered negotiations could leave Kyiv vulnerable to Putin’s demands, while Ukraine has sought stronger backing from its allies on the continent.

“Without Europeans, there is no support for Ukraine,” French President Emmanuel Macron said this week. “There is no more US support.”

Representatives of Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland are expected to participate in the next round of peace talks.

A Queens woman was left in agony after she sought out a traditional Chinese mugwort treatment for pain relief and relaxation, but was left with “severe burns,” according to a lawsuit.

Young Ma alleged workers at Dodam Acupuncture and Pain Clinic in Flushing burned her during a moxibustion treatment in July, according to the suit filed in Queens Supreme Court on Nov. 9.

Moxibustion involves burning dried mugwort — an herb called moxa — on or near specific acupuncture points on the body to stimulate blood flow, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

It’s been used since about 500 B.C.

Ma argued in the lawsuit that the staff at Dodam “negligently” performed the treatment, leaving her with “severe and painful burns.”

Moxa can be applied directly or indirectly.

When applied directly, burning moxa is placed on someone’s skin until they start to feel the heat.

But in the United States, indirect application is most common since it is safer, according to the Virginia University Integrative Medicine.

It is unclear where on her body Ma was burned, although moxibustion is commonly performed on one’s lower back, abdomen, knees, hands and feet.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had no qualms about canoodling with his lover as daughter Madison looked on, according to resurfaced reports in the wake of his stunning ouster from the tech giant he founded.

The jaw-dropping scene unfolded during Huang’s visit to Taiwan in May 2025, when the very married chip tycoon joined lover and alleged CCP spy Alice Huang — a former senior executive at Singapore-based MegaSpeed International — for a dinner party at the exclusive eatery Sanliu Shifu, according to Taiwanese news station TVBS.

During the lively meal, the pair made no attempt to hide their affections, sitting with their arms draped around each other’s waists.

They kept up a steady stream of conversation and laughter with Jensen’s daughter Madison and her hubby-to-be Nico Caprez at the same table, according to Chinese media outlet NetEase.

Alice — the Chinese business exec who US intelligence officials suspect of working for Beijing — even leaned in to give Huang some kisses on the cheek while Madison grabbed a phone from Caprez and snapped off a couple shots of the adorable pair, reported the Taiwan press.

Afterward, the older couple hopped in a car together and sped off.

Whether Madison knew the true nature of her father’s relationship with Alice, 49, is unknown.

The 35-year-old newlywed and culinary school graduate works as Senior Director of Product Marketing, helping manufacturers build and test robotics, at Nvidia.

Hubby Caprez, a former Alpine ski racer for Switzerland, is also a Nvidian, acting as vice president of global AI infrastructure growth at the company, reported the Economic Times.

Huang, 63, has been wed to wife Lori, 64, since 1985, after they met at Oregon State University in the early ’80s. Along with Madison, they are parents to Spencer, 36, who also holds a position at chip giant Nvidia.

The couple split their time between pricey properties in California and Hawaii.

Lori has chosen to stay silent on her hubby’s prickly predicament.

Alice, meanwhile, is at the center of a much bigger controversy.

US intelligence officials reportedly believe the 49-year-old businesswoman was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, with allegations that she was positioned to gather valuable information about the chip giant’s tech empire.

Until recently, the Silicon Valley rock star has kept up a picture-perfect image, courtesy of PR firm Heller — known for handling high-profile public scandals — he had reportedly hired at least a year before admitting to an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy and pressured to resign, according to Taiwanese outlet NetEase.

Madison was also in close contact with the PR image makers, said the NetEase report.

The group kept Huang’s wholesome, devoted family man reputation intact — until it all blew up in their faces.

“I was unfaithful to my wife,” Huang boo-hooed in a company email posted on Nvidia’s website Nov. 8. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

The same day, Nvidia announced that it would investigate whether he was “the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” said a press release.

Huang had also allegedly been involved with Kimberly Powell, 48, Nvidia’s married vice president of health care, along with an additional intimate relationship with another, unidentified Nvidia employee.

On Nov. 12, Huang’s 33-year reign over Nvidia came to a screeching halt when the company announced his resignation as CEO, president and board member.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor.

Huang — who’s estimated to be worth a staggering $143 billion — has also agreed to cooperate with congressional lawmakers seeking answers about his relationship with Alice and the national security threats surrounding their affair.

Video shared by a mall shopkeeper showed teens, parents and other adults sprinting out of the Ontario Mills Mall food court after shots rang out, although the gunfire could not be heard in the footage.

One group of shoppers left in such a hurry that their pizza sat half-eaten on a food court table.

“Brother the mall cleared out in two seconds, they said gun?” one person could be heard saying in the video.

“They left their pizza, y’all left your pizza,” he added, showing two half-eaten pepperoni slices.

A local business owner posted the videos, describing the situation as “so scary,” and saying her heart was “low key pounding.”

Thankfully, no one was hurt, police said. The Ontario Police Department responded to a report of shots fired near Dave & Buster’s and Burlington around 7:07 p.m.

“Ontario PD is actively investigating a shooting at the Ontario Mills Mall. No reported injuries. The scene is contained and a suspect is in custody. There is no threat to the community. Updates to follow,” the department wrote on X at 8:03 p.m.

The suspect was a juvenile, according to ABC7.

“The scene at Ontario Mills is inactive. Suspect is in custody and no one is outstanding. Ontario Mills will resume business as normal,” police wrote.

The cause of the shooting is under investigation. It’s unclear if a weapon has been recovered.

Ontario Mills Mall is located in Ontario, in San Bernardino County. The mall is one of the top shopping destinations in Southern California, with millions of visitors every year.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy revealed investigators are looking into whether a contractor’s error or a faulty router triggered a nationwide ground stop that snarled air traffic and stranded 1 million travelers Friday.

Workers from federal contractor L3 Harris were upgrading communication routers at a “remote location” when the system went down, Duffy said at a press conference Saturday.

“What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence – meaning, was it user error or installator error from L3 Harris — or did they install a faulty router? We haven’t determined what the fault was. Was it the router? Or were they not doing great work for us at L3 Harris?”

The transit boss emphasized that investigators “don’t believe” a cyber attack caused the widespread incident — but didn’t rule out the theory completely.

L3 Harris did not immediately respond to request for comment on the allegations.

This is a breaking story. Please check back for updates.

Daniel Kaluuya and Tyriq Withers are managing to give the internet something else to talk about following the FAA’s nationwide ground stop.

The two actors, who were among the passengers stranded Friday night as planes were grounded across the US, have since gone viral for a bizarre interview inside Eugene Airport in Oregon.

Speaking with KVAL News as the airport descended into chaos, Kaluuya, 37, and Withers, 28, recounted how they were forced to deboard their Los Angeles-bound flight.

“I just want to thank God and the FAA for protecting us, post-blue wave as well,” Withers said, seemingly referring to Democrats’ sweeping victories in the midterm elections, which saw the party take control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

“It’s really upsetting me and my homegirl, ’cause if you can’t go to the airport, where the hell can you go?” he added.

Withers appeared to be referencing a viral 2016 news interview in which a partygoer famously said, “It’s upsetting me and my homegirl, ’cause we feel like, well, damn, if you can’t go to Bella Noche, where the hell can you go?”

The reporter interviewing Kaluuya and Withers couldn’t help but laugh before quickly turning the microphone toward Kaluuya, who said he felt “grateful.”

“Obviously, it’s an inconvenience, but I feel grateful … Think about how many lives were probably saved because of that decision,” he added.

Kaluuya and Withers weren’t the only celebrities caught up in the nationwide ground stop, as “Baywatch” actress Brooks Nader also found herself stranded aboard a private jet amid the unusual travel disruption.

The “Love Thy Nader” television personality, 29, was “literally about to take off” from New York on a flight bound for Louisiana, where she was set to attend an LSU football game, when the alert was sent out, according to TMZ.

The outlet reported that she was “safe” but stranded on the tarmac, with her flight unlikely to depart that evening.

Earlier that day, Nader had shared a selfie to her Instagram Stories from what appeared to be the private jet.

Posing with a peace sign, she included a countdown to her appearance in Baton Rouge.

The FAA (Federal Aviation Administration) announced the unprecedented nationwide ground stop just before 4 p.m. Friday, citing “extraordinary circumstances” and “reasons of safety.”

The agency lifted the ground stop just before 8:30 p.m., roughly four hours after it was issued, following widespread flight delays and cancellations across the U.S.

news.originalContent:
Regulator said Meta’s ‘lack of cooperation’ and the large number of people affected contributed to size of the fine.

Italian regulators have fined Meta 805 million euros ($887m) for accessing users’ photos without their consent.

The Facebook app on Android devices “accessed photos, videos and associated metadata stored on Italian users’ smartphones without specific consent and without informing them”, Garante, the Italian data privacy authority, said Saturday.

The issue relates specifically to the “Get suggestions from gallery when browsing Facebook” feature, which suggests photos and videos from the phone’s gallery for posting while browsing.

This feature violates the Italian law implementing the EU’s ePrivacy directive, the authority said.

Garante said the app’s process for collecting consent is too generic and does not allow users to fully understand the specific permissions they are allowing by accepting. The suggestions option was also enabled by default.

The figure of 805 million euros is by far the largest fine ever imposed by the Italian regulator.

Garante said Meta must fix the unclear consent notification and disable it being set by default, suggesting that roughly 20 million Italian Android users could have been affected by it.

The regulator also highlighted a “lack of cooperation” by Meta and said an earlier violation, which resulted in a 2019 fine, was a contributing factor in their decision.

The amount is roughly 0.47 percent of Meta’s global turnover.

The proceedings did not address the possible use of content to train artificial intelligence, which Meta denies.

Meta has not yet publicly commented on the matter, and it has the right to appeal the regulator’s decision.

news.originalContent:
The EU said that “Israel must enable the work of the UN and its agencies” after the group was blocked access into Gaza.

The European Union has urged Israel to reopen all Gaza border crossings and grant “immediate, unimpeded access” for aid groups to provide humanitarian relief in the territory following devastating flooding in Gaza this week.

Civilian infrastructure and medical facilities in Gaza “must be protected,” said an EU statement released on Saturday by the office of Kaja Kallas, the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and the Vice-President of the European Commission.

The EU call came as an Israeli drone attack killed two more Palestinians in Gaza on Saturday.

The drone struck them as they walked down a street in Jabaliya on the northern edge of Gaza City, according to Mohamed Abu Selmiya, director of Shifa Hospital in Gaza City, where the casualties were taken. The American field hospital said several other people were wounded but did not provide a number.

news.originalContent:
The probe was launched in 1977 but it continues to relay space-related data back to a team of NASA scientists daily.

NASA has announced that its Voyager 1 probe will soon become humanity’s first object to travel one light-day from Earth.

On Wednesday, the robotic space probe will hit the milestone of travelling at least 16 billion miles since its launch in 1977, a distance equal to one light-day, or how far light can travel in 24 hours.

The probe completed its Saturn flyby in 1980, the end of its primary planetary mission, and is currently travelling at roughly 36,000 miles per hour (58km/h) in interstellar space, the vast gap between stars.

NASA expects it to take 18,000 years to travel a full light-year, and double that before it nears another star.

Plutonium-powered Voyager 1 was launched shortly before another probe, Voyager 2. Both continue to relay data back to Earth daily, including readings on the strength and direction of the magnetic field as well as on the surrounding pressure, dust and galactic cosmic rays.

Voyager 2 is expected to hit one light-day from Earth in 2035.

Both are kept active by a skeleton team of NASA engineers who send commands roughly once a week, and more if the probe gets into trouble.

In October, the team briefly lost communication with Voyager 1, and they have not yet figured out why.

Voyager 1 project manager Suzanne Dodd described Voyager 1 as “a national treasure” and told The Associated Press news agency that the two probes’ activities are akin to that of weather satellites.

The probe’s cultural impact has been significant. The famous “Pale Blue Dot” photo of Earth was taken by Voyager 1 in 1990.

“All of us — everyone on Earth — have been touched by these missions,” the Planetary Society’s Bill Nye said in a statement.

news.originalContent:
Steelmaker promises back pay for workers whose layoffs its US owner blamed on tariffs, weak demand and imports.

Canadian steelmaker Stelco says it will recall all 175 workers laid off at its plant in Hamilton and pay them retroactively, following a weeks-long standoff that pitted workers and the Canadian government against its owner in the United States.

The announcement on Friday came shortly after Canada’s Industry Minister Melanie Joly said she would seek a court order to force Cleveland-Cliffs to sell Stelco unless she heard from management by the end of the day.

The company said in a statement on Friday that it had reached agreements with enough customers to restart its finishing operations and that workers would be recalled on December 1. They would receive back pay for the standard wages they would have earned while laid off.

The president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, Ron Wells, welcomed the announcement and credited pressure from workers, the union and the government.

At a news conference, he called the layoffs “illegal” and “immoral” which should never have happened.

Alongside him was Joly, who said the outcome sent a message to investors that Canada was “a country of the rule of law and that the law applies to everyone, notwithstanding the size of your wallet.”

“This fight was absolutely worth it,” she said.

Cleveland-Cliffs, which bought Stelco in 2024, announced in late September that up to 500 workers would be laid off at Stelco’s plants in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ontario, citing weak demand and difficult market conditions for cold-rolled and coated steel products used to make everything from cars to appliances.

It blamed US President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canadian steel, which made it more expensive in the US, as well as competition from cheaper foreign steel, which it argued was eating into domestic demand for Canadian steel.

Ottawa said the layoffs violated binding commitments the company made when it bought Stelco, including keeping the same number of Canadian unionised employees through 2029.

The government and the union also argued that Cleveland-Cliffs’ CEO Lourenco Goncalves violated a commitment to advocate for policies that would benefit the steel industries in both Canada and the US when he publicly supported Trump’s tariffs on steel, including Canada’s.

Goncalves’ open support for the tariffs raised questions, given that he also blamed them for Stelco’s financial troubles.

In its statement, Cleveland-Cliffs said its customers had committed to supporting its operations in Hamilton “despite the lack of response from the federal government to address the shortfalls in their tariff response program.”

It didn’t provide details on the agreements it had reached with customers or explain what had changed to make restarting operations viable.

Cleveland-Cliffs did not respond to a request for comment.

news.originalContent:
The prospect of keeping the Congressional leaders in power is exposing long-running tensions in the party.

Over a week after Democrats rode a historic wave of support to retake the United States Congress, divisions within the party seem to be threatening to undermine its newfound political momentum.

Despite growing calls for a change in Congressional leadership, Democrats Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries appear likely to remain at the helm of their respective US Senate and House caucuses.

After amassing the most Democratic power in Washington since 2009, the two New Yorkers are seeking to retain their leadership positions as their party prepares to take control of both chambers in January.

Schumer, the US Senate’s 75-year-old minority leader, is vying to lead Democrats’ new majority in the chamber, a post he previously held during Joe Biden’s presidency. On the other side of the US Capitol, the 56-year-old Jeffries, as the current minority leader in the US House, is seeking the top role of speaker, placing him second in the line of succession for the US presidency.

But the prospect of keeping Schumer and Jeffries in charge has frustrated some Democrats, exposing long-running tensions between Democratic lawmakers who want to maintain continuity and those who believe their midterm victories offer an opportunity to fundamentally reshape the party’s priorities.

Here’s why Schumer and Jeffries could prevail:

Perhaps the biggest reason the top two Democrats in the US Congress will hold onto their posts: the party’s massive electoral gains.

Schumer’s supporters argue he helped Democrats secure at least eight Republican-held Senate seats, including victories in traditionally conservative states. The party is poised to hold as many as 56 seats in the next Congress, giving it a substantial majority not seen since former President Barack Obama’s first term in office.

“When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give him another contract”, Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego, with Schumer by his side, told reporters on Tuesday. “And this has been a really good election cycle for us”.

Schumer also played a central role in recruiting candidates who could compete in states where Democrats have struggled in recent elections, including former Ohio Senator Sherrod Brown and former North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper.

Adam Jentleson, a longtime US Senate aide and author of, Supermajority: How Democrats Can Build Lasting Power, argued Schumer’s electoral success makes it difficult for critics to mount a successful challenge.

“It’s hard to argue with somebody who just oversaw the biggest election the Democrats have had since Watergate,” Jentleson said during an interview with public radio station WBUR earlier this month.

“The only people who matter are the members of the Democratic caucus,” Jentleson said, explaining that lawmakers who had recently benefitted from the midterm results would have little incentive to remove the person who helped deliver those victories.

Schumer’s allies have made a similar argument. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, who oversees the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, credited Schumer’s candidate recruitment and fundraising efforts for helping the party reclaim the US Senate.

“That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership,” she said.

Schumer himself has expressed confidence that he has enough support to retain the position.

In an interview with The Washington Sun on Wednesday, he said he had secured more than enough backing from his colleagues.

“I am going to be elected leader, OK, and we’re united on the issues,” Schumer told the Sun. “We’re united.”

Not every Democrat believes last week’s victories are enough to anoint Schumer as the party’s leader in the Senate in the next Congress.

Senator Chris Van Hollen announced on Thursday he would mount a challenge for the role after factions of the Democratic base, particularly progressives, have called for new leadership.

The Maryland Democrat attracted attention at the start of US President Donald Trump’s second term after he travelled to El Salvador to meet with his constituent, Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who had been deported to the country despite a judge’s ruling barring his removal.

That, according to a senior Senate Democratic aide who spoke with Al Jazeera, exemplified “the fight Schumer just doesn’t have”.

“This is not about any one individual, but it is about answering the call of the American people,” Van Hollen said during a Thursday appearance on MSNOW, adding that US voters sent a message to “reject the status quo and to reject business as usual”.

Another Senate aide, who would only speak on condition of anonymity to talk freely about an internal matter, suggested Van Hollen’s bid may be more about extracting concessions from Schumer, like a promise to serve as a short-term “bridge” to a new generation of Democratic leadership.

An analysis by Al Jazeera showed that 12 Democratic senators have publicly committed to backing Schumer in next month’s leadership election. At least 10 senators, including independent Bernie Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, have said they will not. However, only half of those opposed to Schumer’s leadership have backed Van Hollen’s challenge.

In an interview with The Nation published on Wednesday, the Vermont independent senator acknowledged knowing Schumer for decades and even liking him personally. But he argued that personal relationships should not determine who leads the party.

“In this moment in American history, Chuck’s views are way out of touch with where the American people are at — and especially with where [the base of] the Democratic Party is,” Sanders said.

He added that Schumer was not in tune with Democratic voters on the issues, arguing the party needed a new and more ambitious direction.

Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin has also questioned Schumer’s leadership, calling for a concrete plan outlining how Democrats intend to use their newly won congressional power.

Slotkin went further on Tuesday, suggesting to reporters at the US Capitol that senators withhold a quorum — the minimum number of lawmakers required to conduct official business — if Schumer runs unopposed, until he presents a plan that gives members a meaningful voice in setting the party’s priorities.

Georgia Senator Raphael Warnock has also declined to commit to supporting Schumer, telling CNN on Tuesday that Democrats are at an “inflection point” and any senator who believes they should lead deserves an opportunity to make their case.

Still, there is a difference between public dissatisfaction and the votes needed to remove a leader. Senate Democrats select their leader through a private ballot, requiring only a simple majority of the caucus.

Tre Easton, vice president for public policy at the Searchlight Institute and a former deputy chief of staff for Democratic Senator John Fetterman, has also questioned the timing of the push against Schumer, arguing calls for new leadership would have carried more weight following the Democrats’ losses in 2024 rather than immediately after their electoral successes in 2026.

“The job of the leader in each legislative chamber here in the U.S. isn’t to articulate a vision for the party”, Easton said in a social media post. “It’s to keep each respective caucus together and count votes. Dassit”.

The outlook is considerably clearer for Jeffries, who is seeking to become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes on January 3.

Unlike Schumer, Jeffries does not face a prominent challenger for his leadership position, despite criticism from some progressives over his approach to Trump and his longstanding support for Israel.

His backing from moderate Democrats has been particularly visible.

The New Democrat Coalition, a group of Democratic centrists representing 142 current and newly elected lawmakers, issued a statement on Tuesday endorsing his bid for speaker.

“Hakeem Jeffries is the right person at the right time to lead our party”, the group said. “He’s smart, strategic, and action-oriented, with strong relationships across the Democratic caucus”.

The coalition added that it “can’t wait to vote for Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker of the House on January 3, 2027”.

But support from the party’s moderate wing has not eliminated dissatisfaction among progressives.

Representative Pramila Jayapal, a former chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said she is withholding her support for Jeffries unless he commits to advancing Medicare for All, a proposal to establish a government-funded universal healthcare system.

Jayapal has also acknowledged that the lack of an alternative candidate complicates the leadership debate.

“You can’t beat somebody with nobody,” the Washington state Democrat told Talking Points Memo, adding that the emergence of a challenger would change the calculations of lawmakers considering whether to support Jeffries.

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, meanwhile, was asked by CNN whether she supported Jeffries.

“The race is unopposed. Yeah,” she responded, suggesting that the absence of a challenger was an important factor in the debate.

The tensions in the US House have also been illustrated by the case of Don Leonard, an incoming Democratic congressman from Ohio who said he will withhold his support for Jeffries unless the party commits to specific policy changes.

Leonard, who has called for an end to US support for Israel and the war in Iran, alleged in a video posted to social media that senior House Democrats threatened to make his life a “living hell” in Washington and undermine his chances of re-election in 2028 if he continued attaching conditions to his support for Jeffries.

He has not identified the lawmakers involved, and the allegations have not been independently verified. House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar told reporters on Tuesday he did not know which senior Democrats Leonard was referring to.

Jeffries, who has denied reports that US House Democrats have been receiving calls to oppose his bid for the speakership, spoke to reporters on Thursday about frustrations within the party over his leadership.

“We take nothing for granted, because all of us in the House of Representatives are on a two-year employment contract”, Jeffries said. “And we have to continue to make our case both with respect to our track record up until this point, as well as, perhaps even more importantly, our vision for the future”.

The leadership contests are scheduled for November 18 and 19 for House Democrats and at an unannounced date in December for Senate Democrats.

If elected, both Schumer and Jeffries will likely continue to face competing demands from progressives seeking more aggressive action against Trump and from moderates representing districts and states where a more centrist approach may be politically important.

They will also have to contend with the practical limitations of governing. Even with control of both chambers, Democrats will not have the 60 Senate votes generally required to overcome a filibuster, meaning they will need Republican support for much of their legislation.

For now, however, the party’s electoral gains have given Schumer and Jeffries an argument for continuity.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” Schumer wrote in an X post on Thursday. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader.”

The coalition added that it “can’t wait to vote for Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker of the House on January 3, 2027”.

But support from the party’s moderate wing has not eliminated dissatisfaction among progressives.

Representative Pramila Jayapal, a former chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said she is withholding her support for Jeffries unless he commits to advancing Medicare for All, a proposal to establish a government-funded universal healthcare system.

Jayapal has also acknowledged that the lack of an alternative candidate complicates the leadership debate.

“You can’t beat somebody with nobody,” the Washington state Democrat told Talking Points Memo, adding that the emergence of a challenger would change the calculations of lawmakers considering whether to support Jeffries.

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, meanwhile, was asked by CNN whether she supported Jeffries.

“The race is unopposed. Yeah,” she responded, suggesting that the absence of a challenger was an important factor in the debate.

The tensions in the US House have also been illustrated by the case of Don Leonard, an incoming Democratic congressman from Ohio who said he will withhold his support for Jeffries unless the party commits to specific policy changes.

Leonard, who has called for an end to US support for Israel and the war in Iran, alleged in a video posted to social media that senior House Democrats threatened to make his life a “living hell” in Washington and undermine his chances of re-election in 2028 if he continued attaching conditions to his support for Jeffries.

He has not identified the lawmakers involved, and the allegations have not been independently verified. House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar told reporters on Tuesday he did not know which senior Democrats Leonard was referring to.

Jeffries, who has denied reports that US House Democrats have been receiving calls to oppose his bid for the speakership, spoke to reporters on Thursday about frustrations within the party over his leadership.

“We take nothing for granted, because all of us in the House of Representatives are on a two-year employment contract”, Jeffries said. “And we have to continue to make our case both with respect to our track record up until this point, as well as, perhaps even more importantly, our vision for the future”.

The leadership contests are scheduled for November 18 and 19 for House Democrats and at an unannounced date in December for Senate Democrats.

If elected, both Schumer and Jeffries will likely continue to face competing demands from progressives seeking more aggressive action against Trump and from moderates representing districts and states where a more centrist approach may be politically important.

They will also have to contend with the practical limitations of governing. Even with control of both chambers, Democrats will not have the 60 Senate votes generally required to overcome a filibuster, meaning they will need Republican support for much of their legislation.

For now, however, the party’s electoral gains have given Schumer and Jeffries an argument for continuity.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” Schumer wrote in an X post on Thursday. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader.”

news.originalContent:
اداره هوانوردی فدرال آمریکا، پس از متوقف کردن تمامی پروازها که منجر به سرگردانی شمار زیادی از مسافران در فرودگاه‌ها شده بود، حریم هوایی کشور را بازگشایی کرد.

بر اساس گزارش‌ها، توقف پروازها در روز جمعه منجر به تاخیر در بیش از ۸۵۰۰ پرواز و لغو نزدیک به ۸۰۰۰ پرواز شد.

وب‌سایت «فلایت رادار» که پروازها را رصد می‌کند، گفته است که تا روز شنبه نزدیک به ۱۰ هزار پرواز به مقصد یا از مبدا فرودگاه‌های آمریکا لغو شده‌اند.

اگرچه حریم هوایی اکنون بازگشایی شده است اما در حالی که فرودگاه‌ها در تلاش هستند تا به انبوه پروازهای به تاخیر افتاده رسیدگی کنند، بسیاری از مسافران همچنان سرگردان خواهند ماند.

شان دافی، وزیر حمل‌ونقل آمریکا، گفت که بازگشت پروازها به روال عادی، روندی کند خواهد داشت و  پیامدهای این اختلال تا چند روز ادامه خواهد داشت.

او علت این مشکل را فشار بیش از حد بر سیستم دانست و آن را ناشی از کمبود سرمایه‌گذاری بلندمدت در بخش کنترل ترافیک هوایی عنوان کرد.

او گفت: «در حال حاضر مراکز کنترل ما فعال هستند اما از سرگیری پروازها به منابع موجود بستگی دارد.

شان دافی افزود که «مدتی طول می‌کشد تا بتوانیم وضعیت پیش‌آمده در بعدازظهر امروز را سامان دهیم.»

آقای دافی توضیح داد که این قطعی، پیامدهای زنجیره‌ای به دنبال خواهد داشت و گفت که در حال بررسی پروازهای آخر هفته هستند تا بتوانند اوضاع را به روال عادی بازگردانند؛ از این رو، مشکلات ناشی از این اختلال تا چند روز ادامه خواهد داشت.

پیش از این مارک‌وین مولین، وزیر امنیت داخلی، اعلام کرد که هیچ‌گونه شواهدی مبنی بر وقوع حمله سایبری وجود ندارد.

رئیس پیشین هیئت ملی ایمنی حمل‌ونقل در آمریکا می‌گوید از زمان حملات ۱۱ سپتامبر ۲۰۰۱، چنین توقف گسترده‌ای در پروازها در آمریکا سابقه نداشته است.

رابرت ال. ساموالت به شبکه خبری سی‌بی‌اس، شریک رسانه‌ای بی‌بی‌سی در آمریکا، گفت: «واقعاً باورنکردنی است که چنین اتفاقی در عصر حاضر رخ می‌دهد.»

او اشاره کرد که در سال ۲۰۲۳ نیز توقف کوتاه‌مدتی در پروازها رخ داده بود که تنها چند ساعت به طول انجامید.

تئو لگت، خبرنگار بی‌بی‌سی می‌گوید که سیستم‌های کنترل ترافیک هوایی ایالات متحده به بسیار کهنه و قدیمی بودن شهرت دارند. سال گذشته، کنگره آمریکا ۱۲/۵ میلیارد دلار را برای به‌روزرسانی این سیستم‌ها تصویب کرد، اما به بودجه بسیار بیشتری نیاز است.

این تنها دومین مورد از چنین توقف سراسری‌ بود که از زمان حوادث ۱۱ سپتامبر ۲۰۰۱ رخ داد.

دکتر گای گراتون، دانشیار حوزه هوانوردی در دانشگاه کرنفیلد، به بی‌بی‌سی گفت: «به نظر می‌رسد این بدترین مورد بعد از ۱۱ سپتامبر ۲۰۰۱  باشد، هرچند قطعاً در آن مقیاس نیست.»

دکتر گراتون همچنین به توقف پروازها در ایالات متحده در سال ۲۰۲۳ اشاره کرد که به دلیل نقص فنی در سامانه «اطلاعیه‌ها و پیام‌های فوری هوانوردی»  رخ داده بود.

او گفت: «آن حادثه یک ساعت و ۵۲ دقیقه به طول انجامید، باعث تأخیر در حدود ۹۵۰۰ پرواز شد و حدود ۱۳۰۰ پرواز را لغو کرد.»

در جریان اختلال سال ۲۰۲۳، امکان انتشار اطلاعیه‌های ایمنی ترافیک هوایی وجود نداشت و تا زمان بازیابی آن سامانه، پروازها متوقف شدند.

اما حادثه روز جمعه، طولانی‌تر از رویداد سال ۲۰۲۳ بود.

news.originalContent:
(Photo by Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has ordered a “ground stop” at all U.S. airports until further notice.

The FAA’s Air Traffic Control System Command Center (ATCSCC) announced the nationwide ground stop Friday, citing safety concerns in ATCSCC Advisory 111.

“Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center, all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case-by-case basis,” according to the announcement.

In response to the reports of the outage, an FAA spokesperson in a statement to the Caller confirmed the ground stop, writing, “The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide updates.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote in a post on X on Friday that the FAA had issued a nationwide ground stop at all U.S. airports due to a communications issue affecting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.

“The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them,” Duffy wrote.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

A Washington state teen suffered a severe brain injury when she was flung from the sunroof of a car she was standing in during a parking lot stunt.

Elexis Robinson, 17, was hanging halfway out of the top of a car when the driver made a sharp turn, tossing the teen girl out of the moving vehicle and onto the hard pavement in Vancouver, Wash., on Nov. 3.

The teen was with friends in a shopping center’s parking lot just after 8 p.m. when she crashed head-first in the near-death experience, KGW reported.

Robinson fractured her skull and developed three near-fatal brain bleeds – one on the right side and two on the left – her mother, Tricha Linares, revealed on a GoFundMe page.

“As a mother, there are simply no words to describe the fear, heartbreak, and helplessness of watching your child endure something so devastating,” Linares wrote. “In a matter of moments, our entire world was turned upside down.”

Skid marks covered a large section of the parking lot, a result of what appears to be a common activity by thrill seekers in the area, according to drone video from the outlet.

Robinson was diagnosed with a severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) that will leave her hospitalized and needing extensive rehabilitation.

“The daughter we love so dearly is now facing an unimaginable medical battle, and our family is desperately hoping, praying, and holding onto every bit of hope for her recovery,” the heartbroken mother added.

Robinson, described as a talented high school senior two credits shy of graduation, now has trouble remembering basic information, including her name, due to her injury.

“Elexis is so much more than this tragedy. She is an incredibly intelligent, beautiful, and kindhearted young woman who has worked so hard throughout high school and is on track to graduate with honors,” Linares wrote.

“She has an entire future ahead of her, dreams waiting to be fulfilled, and so much life left to live. She is deeply loved, and we are determined to stand beside her through every step of this journey.”

The teen spends most of the day sleeping and when she is awake is usually confused, emotional and disoriented, her mother said.

Doctors won’t be able to give a prognosis on Robinson’s long-term condition for some time, stretching between six months and a year.

“We’re kind of left in the dark of what’s going to happen,” Linares said.

The mother blamed her daughter’s new friendship for the almost fatal accident.

“This girl also made a mistake, too. This is her choice, just as much as it was my daughter’s choice to make a mistake,” Linares added. “I want her to learn the consequences of this, but she is a 17-year-old girl as well, and to have her life completely ruined and destroyed, I don’t need two lives like that. I don’t.”

news.originalContent:
The vote, first expected in 2022, will now be held on February 11, according to the country’s election commission.

South Sudan has delayed its first-ever presidential and parliamentary elections until February, the latest in a series of delays to the long-sought vote, as ethnic and political tensions deepen.

The country’s election commission announced on Saturday that the polls would be held on February 11 next year, instead of December 22 this year. It did not give any reason for the decision.

The world’s youngest country, which continues to grapple with violence despite a 2018 peace deal that ended five years of civil war, has delayed the vote at least three times since setting 2022 as its election year.

In September, South Sudan’s President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional unity government and appointed a caretaker administration. That step allowed the country to move towards elections without first completing a permanent constitution or census – two processes that were previously tied to the transition.

But analysts and watchdogs warned that move dismantled a key power-sharing arrangement, consolidating power in Kiir’s hands and raising the risk of renewed widespread conflict.

“This amounts to a constitutional coup through legislative reforms,” Yasmin Sooka, chair of the United Nations Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan, said in October.

“Whether elections take place or not, South Sudan will still need an inclusive political settlement, protection for civilians and institutions capable of preventing further violence,” she added.

Kiir’s government forces and followers of detained former Vice President Riek Machar have been involved in escalating, deadly confrontations in recent months.

Other ethnic tensions and cattle-rustling battles have also complicated the picture in one of the world’s poorest countries.

South Sudan became independent from Sudan in 2011, but Kiir’s and Machar’s forces fought a civil war from 2013 to 2018 that killed at least 400,000 people.

Machar has been under house arrest since last March, accused of crimes against humanity.

Under the new election timetable, voter registration is due to begin on Saturday, November 14 and continue until November 28.

A 45-day election campaign period will run from December 27 to February 9, followed by a one-day silence period before the February 11 poll.

Gabriel Bol Deng, chairman of the National Elections Commission, said a total of 3,161 registration centres have been set up across the country, with more than 22,000 staff recruited for the operation.

According to the World Bank, about 90 percent of South Sudan’s 15 million inhabitants have no state-recognised identification, complicating their registration.

Such people, particularly in rural areas, will be identified by community leaders and issued an “identification form” enabling them to vote, Deng said.

news.originalContent:

Podcaster Joe Rogan on Friday blasted the idea that podcasters should be taken as seriously as journalists and participate in White House press briefings, declaring, “We talk s—!”

Rogan spoke with comedians Shane Gillis, Mark Normand and Ari Shaffir, joking about how chaotic President Trump’s recent press gaggles have been, especially given the nature of the format.

“There is a problem at these things,” Rogan said. “Like, say if you have a question and you’re talking to him. Someone else would just talk louder right next to you with a totally different question. It is f—ing annoying. And they don’t care. It’s a bad podcast!”

“It’s a bad podcast,” Rogan repeated. “If you hear a guy with a good question, let him go. Let him cook. Let him ask his f—ing question. And if you have a question later, raise your f—ing hand. And when he comes to you, ask your question.

“But if you’re just yelling over the other guy’s question, a louder, different question. That s—‘s annoying.”

Rogan contrasted this with David Sacks, chairman of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, recalling Sacks’ complaint that the administration had lost the podcasters with recent policies and ought to have given them a front-row seat at news conferences.

“Like, hey, how about no?” Rogan responded. “How about real journalists? How about not have us do that? Also, we’re not going! We’re not going to the f—ing press conferences and sitting in the front row and asking questions to Karoline Leavitt.”

“We’re not going to go to the press conferences,” he continued.

“We’re not press people. We talk s—. OK? And it’s a sickness of our society that people take our opinions so importantly that it’s so significant. It should not be. They do though, unfortunately. And it works, unfortunately.”

Podcasters played a prominent role in the 2024 presidential election, with Rogan interviewing Trump and later endorsing him.

The 2024 campaign was nicknamed the “podcast election” as candidates sought to reach voters through podcasts and other alternative media platforms.

Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt was credited with opening up the briefing room to alternative media outlets during her tenure by creating a “new media seat.”

The seat, located at the front of the room and just steps from the podium, allowed bloggers, social media influencers and others to ask questions of the White House press secretary during briefings.

news.originalContent:
World number two Sabalenka’s campaign at the WTA Finals came to a disappointing end after she failed to the reach the semifinals of the season-ending championships.

Elina Svitolina overwhelmed Aryna Sabalenka in the deciding set to seal a ⁠6-3, 3-6, 6-1 upset on Friday and reach the semifinals of the season-ending WTA Finals in Indian Wells, where she will face Linda Noskova.

Svitolina absorbed and redirected Sabalenka’s power effectively, breaking the ⁠Belarusian six times before sealing her first victory over her opponent in more than six years with a forehand winner on her fourth match point.

With the win, Svitolina improved to 2-6 against Sabalenka in their career meetings.

“It was a bit of a roller-coaster match,” Svitolina told reporters.

“I played well in ‌the first set but lost a little bit of rhythm. She played well in the second and served much better. I was really happy with the way I could come back in the third after losing the first game.”

The Ukrainian again did not shake hands with Sabalenka after the match, maintaining her policy of not doing so with Russian and Belarusian players following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Svitolina, the 2018 WTA Finals champion, will face Noskova on ⁠Saturday for a place in the final.

The defeat ended Sabalenka’s season ⁠on a disappointing note.

The second seed won Brisbane International in January and then Indian Wells and the Miami Open in March to complete the “Sunshine Double” but did not claim another title after that.

Sabalenka also surrendered the world number one ⁠ranking to Elena Rybakina at the US Open.

She had entered the season finale among the favourites after Rybakina withdrew on the eve of ⁠the tournament because of illness.

Sabalenka declined to speak to the ⁠media following Friday’s loss.

Earlier in the day, tournament debutant Andreeva continued her impressive run with a 6-2, 6-1 win over fellow Russian Diana Shnaider, her third straight-sets victory of the week.

Shnaider, Andreeva’s friend and doubles partner, replaced Karolina Muchova, who ‌withdrew before the final day of round-robin matches with a gastrointestinal illness.

Andreeva had already secured her place in the semifinals before facing Shnaider and will meet American Jessica Pegula on Saturday.

The eight-day, $10m ‌tournament was moved from Riyadh to Indian Wells Tennis Garden due to the United States-Israeli war on Iran. The event will be played in Charlotte starting next year.

news.originalContent:
Israel’s far right is accused of embedding a hardline agenda so deeply that reversing it may prove almost impossible.

As Israel’s opposition looks to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, speculation has centred on the possible fate of the current government’s more hardline, right-wing elements, including the parties led by the unapologetically pro-settler Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, convicted of inciting terrorism.

While all members of Netanyahu’s cabinet, with the unflinching backing of the opposition politicians hoping to supplant them, have supported Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and attacks on regional states, it is Smotrich and Ben-Gvir who have been the focus of international attention and lightning rods for criticism by Western governments.

With talk of Netanyahu looking to form a unity government with Eisenkot, both ministers have publicly opposed a government led by the former chief-of-staff.

In the run-up to the vote, Ben-Gvir took the unusual step of claiming that Netanyahu now has a choice of selecting himself to “save Israel”, or Eisenkot.

Smotrich, meanwhile, has warned his ultra-Orthodox political allies against entering negotiations with Eisenkot, saying he will “dump them” once he uses their votes to oust Netanyahu.

Netanyahu formed a coalition government with Ben-Gvir’s far-right Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) and Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party in 2022, giving both several of Israel’s most important cabinet positions. Smotrich became finance minister, granting him control over the Israeli budget and a number of institutions in the occupied West Bank, while Ben-Gvir was named national security minister.

Drawing on a wellspring of hardline Zionism, Jewish supremacy and what critics describe as unapologetic racism, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have exploited their political leverage to advance Israel’s most hardline policies over the past three years. They have also transformed their ministries to reflect their hardline ideological projects.

Both have been enthusiastic proponents of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, repeatedly threatening to withdraw their support from the government when it appeared Netanyahu might falter in the face of international pressure about the huge number of civilians killed, famine, and withholding of aid.

In September 2025, Ben-Gvir threatened to bring down the government if Hamas remained in existence following the release of the captives under United States President Donald Trump’s proposed Gaza plan. Both ministers have repeatedly called for the annexation, settlement and ethnic cleansing of Gaza.

Smotrich has encouraged the expansion of illegal settlements within the West Bank and, in the eyes of his opponents, bears culpability for the explosion of settler violence and pogroms across the occupied territory.

In June 2025, Smotrich and Ben-Gvir were sanctioned by a wave of Western countries. Ireland and the Netherlands imposed travel bans on the two ministers, while other countries froze their assets. Irish Taoiseach Micheal Martin said these measures were taken due to their shared “desire to see the elimination of Palestinians from Palestine”.

However, analysts said the ministers and their movements should not be treated as a homogeneous entity or be isolated from Israeli policy in general.

“I would argue that we should not treat Ben-Gvir and Smotrich as a single bloc, since exclusion from government would affect them in opposite ways,” Arie Perliger, of the University of Massachusetts Lowell, who has led studies into the far right in Israel, Europe and the US, told Al Jazeera. “Ben-Gvir’s power is populist and performative, and opposition suits him.”

Ben-Gvir’s roots in the outlawed Kahanist movement had, in tandem with many right-wing movements, relied upon their historical exclusion from power as evidence of a betrayal by the establishment, he added.

Smotrich, meanwhile, had used his position as finance minister to co-opt part of the settlement programme and force through his explicitly Zionist agenda. This means he would have more to lose if he were “cut off from budgets, portfolios and control over settlement policy”.

“Smotrich’s case is the reverse. His achievements were bureaucratic rather than rhetorical,” Perliger said.

Both figures have been accused of transforming their ministries in ways that will linger long after they leave government.

As part of the 2022 deal with Netanyahu that secured his finance portfolio, Smotrich was given the additional role as a minister in the Ministry of Defence. This gave him sweeping powers over much of the occupied West Bank’s Israeli-led civilian administration.

From there, he used his position to establish a separate Settlement Administration and to rapidly accelerate illegal settlement expansion across the occupied territory. In August 2025, he announced the revival of the E1 settlement plan, which he boasted would bury “the idea of a Palestinian state”.

Ben-Gvir has been accused of rapidly politicising the Israeli police force under his command and essentially fashioning it to mirror his own hard-right outlook. He has also introduced sweeping changes to the prison service, including severe restrictions on the conditions and rights of Palestinian prisoners, whose institutional legacy could last for years.

“These are personnel, procedures and facts on the ground and reversing them requires sustained political will,” Perliger added. He is sceptical that an opposition government would override the changes introduced by the ministers.

Ejecting the pair from the mainstream of Israeli politics was also unlikely to dent support for the groups, according to Roi Zur, an assistant professor in the Department of Government at Essex University.

Smotrich’s Religious Zionist movement goes back to the war of 1967 and, together with Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit, has the support of about 10 percent of the Israeli electorate.

“They are stable and will be there for many years … [They] cater to very similar kinds of people in Israel,” Zur told Al Jazeera.

Israel’s far right is accused of embedding a hardline agenda so deeply that reversing it may prove almost impossible.

As Israel’s opposition looks to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, speculation has centred on the possible fate of the current government’s more hardline, right-wing elements, including the parties led by the unapologetically pro-settler Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, convicted of inciting terrorism.

While all members of Netanyahu’s cabinet, with the unflinching backing of the opposition politicians hoping to supplant them, have supported Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and attacks on regional states, it is Smotrich and Ben-Gvir who have been the focus of international attention and lightning rods for criticism by Western governments.

With talk of Netanyahu looking to form a unity government with Eisenkot, both ministers have publicly opposed a government led by the former chief-of-staff.

In the run-up to the vote, Ben-Gvir took the unusual step of claiming that Netanyahu now has a choice of selecting himself to “save Israel”, or Eisenkot.

Smotrich, meanwhile, has warned his ultra-Orthodox political allies against entering negotiations with Eisenkot, saying he will “dump them” once he uses their votes to oust Netanyahu.

Netanyahu formed a coalition government with Ben-Gvir’s far-right Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) and Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party in 2022, giving both several of Israel’s most important cabinet positions. Smotrich became finance minister, granting him control over the Israeli budget and a number of institutions in the occupied West Bank, while Ben-Gvir was named national security minister.

They have also transformed their ministries to reflect their hardline ideological projects.

Both have been enthusiastic proponents of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, repeatedly threatening to withdraw their support from the government when it appeared Netanyahu might falter in the face of international pressure about the huge number of civilians killed, famine, and withholding of aid.

In September 2025, Ben-Gvir threatened to bring down the government if Hamas remained in existence following the release of the captives under United States President Donald Trump’s proposed Gaza plan. Both ministers have repeatedly called for the annexation, settlement and ethnic cleansing of Gaza.

Smotrich has encouraged the expansion of illegal settlements within the West Bank and, in the eyes of his opponents, bears culpability for the explosion of settler violence and pogroms across the occupied territory.

In June 2025, Smotrich and Ben-Gvir were sanctioned by a wave of Western countries. Ireland and the Netherlands imposed travel bans on the two ministers, while other countries froze their assets. news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Microsoft said ​on Saturday that services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook and its other products, ending a global outage that crippled online communications for businesses and governments for over 24 hours.

“We have completed ‌our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions,” the company posted on X.

Microsoft had said server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant, and that it was not aware of any malicious activity, ruling out AI as the cause.

Outlook and Teams are two of the most widely used workplace applications with hundreds of millions of users.

The outage prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending emails, managing calendars and hosting virtual ​meetings.

It affected government agencies from Australia and Japan to the United States, caused delays at trading firms, hindered some companies from publishing earnings and prompted airlines to warn customers of communication lags, according to ​public statements.

Organizations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared.

The outage, reports of which started climbing around ⁠12:25 p.m. ET on Thursday according to Ookla, is one of the longest in Microsoft’s history and the second disruption to its services this year.

Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online — its cloud-based email and ​scheduling hub — leaving unconnected applications operational.

The incident deepens questions about the global reliance on a handful of Big Tech companies that supply both the essential software and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it.

It also highlighted the dependence on Microsoft’s ​workplace software, with outage reports spiking as employees began their workdays across Asia and Europe, according to Downdetector’s parent company, Ookla.

Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million reports worldwide, peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute, more than 1,500 times normal levels.

“It shows how much of the working day now runs through one provider’s email and collaboration tools,” said Luke Kehoe, lead industry analyst at Ookla.

Microsoft shares closed flat at $523.88 on Friday. The stock has gained roughly 8% so far this year.

Disruptions and financial losses from the outage could ​result in numerous insurance claims, but the overall hit to insurers is expected to be limited, said Mario De Cicco, vice president of European financial institutions at Morningstar DBRS.

De Cicco estimated global insured losses from the incident at ​between $300 million and $500 million, well below the $400 million to $1.5 billion financial toll from the 2024 CrowdStrike outage that crashed more than 8 million Windows-based computers and caused widespread disruptions.

Microsoft also faced an outage with its 365 services in January this year and in ‌October last year. Last ⁠month, it reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that impacted its suite of productivity software and a range of industries worldwide.

“The bigger worry is that this is not the first Microsoft 365 outage this year,” said Josh Gilbert, a market analyst at trading platform eToro.

“If reliability starts to look like a recurring problem, it hands every IT department a reason to think twice before putting even more of their business in one provider’s hands.”

Still, some analysts have questioned whether such incidents can push customers on to rivals due to the steep switching costs of replacing tools embedded so deeply in daily operations.

A spokesperson for the UK government said it ​was working with Microsoft to find a solution for ​the outage that hit organizations such as the ⁠NHS and London’s Metropolitan Police.

Lack of access to emails and other services was impacting the Metropolitan Police’s ability to report some crimes online, though its ability to respond to calls was not affected.

The NHS said its local services were turning to alternate measures such as using IT systems or paper records.

For businesses, the fallout was widespread.

European exchange operator ​Euronext reported email disruptions, British insurer Aviva activated backups for its earnings calls and Danish shipping giant Maersk warned customers of delayed updates.

American AI giants OpenAI and ​Anthropic also faced issues with Microsoft ⁠connectors that were later resolved, while Indian airlines IndiGo, Akasa Air and Air India said their email support services were impacted.

The outage also disrupted fund management at Taiwanese securities firms, life insurers, and investment trust companies. One of the companies went as far as canceling a bond repurchase transaction, a source familiar with the situation told Reuters.

Another Taiwanese financial company resorted to using fax to confirm trades, a second source said.

In the US, electric truck maker Workhorse Group rescheduled its results ⁠on Thursday to ​November 16, while Switzerland’s Richemont briefly delayed its first-half results announcement on Friday.

In Australia, where the spy agency and federal police were among organizations ​caught in the outage, Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said Microsoft does not suspect a cyberattack.

“The impact that they are dealing with … is very much on email systems,” the minister added.

news.originalContent:
Analysts say the pact, agreed amid the US-Iran war, aims to deter attacks rather than build an offensive alliance.

Qatar and Turkiye have welcomed a new mutual defence agreement that commits them to a common position against any external armed attack on either country.

The pact followed Friday’s high-level meeting of the Turkiye-Qatar Supreme Strategic Committee in Istanbul, chaired by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.

It comes as the region deals with the fallout of the United States-Israeli war on Iran and disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

So what is in the agreement, and why does it matter now? Here’s what you need to know:

According to a joint communique, the deal aims to strengthen collective defence, promote regional security and establish a common position against external armed attacks targeting either or both countries.

It reflects “not only the commitment of its signatories to safeguarding their sovereignty and territorial integrity, but also their shared vision of contributing to a more secure and stable regional order”, the statement said.

The two countries agreed to consult one another on security threats and defence policy. They also agreed to expand joint military exercises, defence industry collaboration and personnel training exchanges.

The communique, as reported, did not set out what could trigger the agreement or what form a joint response would take.

Other agreements reached at the meeting covered education, consumer protection, and peace, reconciliation and conflict resolution, Qatar’s Al Raya newspaper said in an editorial on Saturday.

Not an offensive one, analysts say.

Abdulla Banndar Al-Etaibi, an assistant professor in the Department of International Affairs at Qatar University, told Al Jazeera that the goal is not to form an alliance against any particular country.

Instead, he said, it is meant to raise the cost of any potential aggression so that others are deterred from attempting it.

He said cooperation already rests on an extended military partnership, including a Turkish military presence, joint training and defence manufacturing.

The partnership is moving to a more advanced level, based on converging security doctrines and a shared view of where threats come from and how to deal with them, said Al-Etaibi.

The region is braced for more conflict.

There are fears of a renewed military escalation, pushing states to build up their defences and deterrence, Al-Etaibi said.

The deal comes amid Israel’s aggressive military posture and growing questions over the future reliability of the US security umbrella.

Regional states are looking to new alliances built on deterrence, joint arms manufacturing and less dependence on outside powers.

In the communique, Ankara and Doha said the war on Iran and its regional repercussions must be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy.

They called for “the swift and full resumption of safe, secure and unimpeded passage through the Strait of Hormuz”.

Because supply chains have become a weak point.

Al-Etaibi said disruption to navigation in Hormuz has made it harder to rely on foreign military supply chains.

Producing weapons locally and securing spare parts is now a strategic necessity, not just an economic choice, he said.

Mahjoob Zweiri, an academic and Middle East policy expert, told Al Jazeera that the move to joint manufacturing marks an advanced strategic stage.

Military industries require billions of dollars of investment and long-term commitments, he said, as well as mutual trust over technology transfer. He said the war had shown why countries need their own manufacturing capacity, pointing to Iran, which kept fighting by producing much of its weaponry at home.

The communique also welcomed the Badr memorandum, signed by Turkiye, Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia.

It described the memorandum as a step towards collective defence through “the development of indigenous capabilities”, including joint production, technology development, information sharing and stronger supply chains.

They hold very close ties.

The Supreme Strategic Committee was set up under an agreement signed on December 19, 2014, according to Anadolu. Friday’s meeting was the 12th such forum.

Al Raya described it as a key framework for monitoring agreements and expanding cooperation.

Zweiri said the new pact reflects a high level of trust between Doha and Ankara after a series of political and security tests the relationship has faced since 2014.

The relationship goes well beyond defence.

Turkish contracting companies have carried out 206 projects in Qatar worth $20.8bn, according to the communique.

The two countries also reiterated a target to raise bilateral trade to $5bn and pledged closer cooperation on energy, particularly liquefied natural gas.

On security, they pledged to counter “terrorism in all its forms and manifestations”.

Possibly drones and air defence.

Ozcan Tikit, a foreign affairs analyst at Anadolu, said the partnership combines Turkish industrial and military expertise with Qatari financial and diplomatic strength.

He expects cooperation to expand to missile defence systems, drones, and armoured vehicles, with Qatar possibly joining advanced Turkish air defence projects.

He said several manufacturing projects could also extend to Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

However, he stressed that these were future possibilities, not projects whose details were announced in the agreement.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

A bomb threat at an ethanol plant prompted a large-scale evacuation of parts of an Illinois city Friday night as officials worked to defuse the credible threat.

The suspicious package was discovered at the BioUrja Renewables plant in Peoria, Ill., just after 1 p.m. Friday.

Peoria police ruled the device a credible threat an hour later as FBI agents were called to the scene, Police Chief Brad Dixon said at a press conference early Saturday morning.

Officials determined a 1-mile-wide blast-radius zone and issued an urgent evacuation notice for the area at 7 p.m.

“As a precautionary measure, the Peoria Police Department is urging anyone who lives or works within a one-mile radius of the facility to immediately evacuate their homes and businesses until further notice,” city officials said.

Bomb technicians were called in and “rendered the package safe” at 9:12 p.m.

The rest of the plant was not cleared and a search for additional threats was launched.

“It’s a large facility. There’s going to be an exhaustive search of the facility. That has not been completed yet,” Dixon said, warning Peoria residents the evacuation notice would remain in effect.

Multiple local, state and federal agencies responded to the bomb threat, including the Illinois State Police, the Illinois Secretary of State, the ATF and the FBI, FBI Springfield Field Office’s Special Agent in Charge Ryan Presley said at the press conference.

news.originalContent:
An ex-minister faces a bribery probe as Hungary’s new government investigates alleged corruption during former Prime Minister Viktor Orban’s rule.

Hungarian investigators have found $19.5m in hidden cash, including bundles dug out in forests, during a corruption probe involving a former minister under ex-Prime Minister Viktor Orban.

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, a new agency set up to investigate suspected misuse of public money, said in a statement late on Friday that searches took place on November 12 and 13 in Budapest and three other parts of Hungary.

Its investigators found Hungarian forints, euros and US dollars in farm buildings, warehouses, a home and “a high-value safe in a secluded location”, as well as beneath the ground in forests. The agency released footage showing officers digging outdoors after dark and examining piles of cash, which was later deposited with the state treasury.

Finance Minister Andras Karman said on Facebook on Friday that 12 treasury employees spent eight hours counting it.

The discovery comes amid an investigation into Miklos Sesztak, Hungary’s development minister from 2014 to 2018, who is suspected of receiving more than $37.2m in bribes and kickbacks tied to overpriced secondhand bus purchases by a state transport company and government construction projects.

He was detained in September and denies wrongdoing.

Prime Minister Peter Magyar, whose centre-right, pro-European Tisza party ended Orban’s 16 years in power in April, said on Facebook on Friday that the recovery signalled the end of what he called the “Fidesz-KDNP mafia”.

Fidesz is Orban’s right-wing party, while KDNP, the Christian Democratic People’s Party, was its smaller governing ally.

Orban has previously accused the new government of using the investigations to force him out of politics.

Other former ministers have been arrested in separate cases, as has Gyorgy Matolcsy, the former governor of Hungary’s central bank, which sets monetary policy.

His case concerns alleged misuse of public assets held by a central bank foundation. Matolcsy has denied wrongdoing.

A survey published this week by Hungarian news website HVG by pollster Median suggested that 70 percent of respondents considered investigating suspected corruption under Orban and holding those responsible accountable very important.

Brotherly love is back in play.

Aaron Rodgers has surprisingly reunited with his younger brother Jordan after years of family tension and estrangement.

The Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback, 42, posed arm-in-arm with Jordan, 38, on Friday at Acrisure Stadium in Pittsburgh, where Jordan was working as a college football analyst for ESPN.

“Great to see little bro @jrodgers11 in his element tonight @acrisurestadium. Really proud of how hard he’s worked to get to where he is now 👊🏻,” Aaron captioned the Instagram snap.

Aaron wore a gray sweater, black pants and a baseball cap for the casual meeting, while Jordan wore a black blazer and blue tie as he covered Pitt’s game against Florida State.

The brothers’ rift became public in 2016 when Jordan appeared on his now-wife JoJo Fletcher’s season of “The Bachelorette” and revealed that Aaron would not be attending his hometown visit since they were estranged.

Aaron later took issue with his younger brother discussing their family troubles on television, saying in July 2016 that it was “a little inappropriate [for Jordan] to talk publicly about some family matter.”

The NFL star was also invited to Jordan and Fletcher’s 2022 wedding in Mexico, but did not attend.

There have been signs of progress this year, however, as Jordan recently made a rare public show of support for his big-name brother during an appearance on ESPN’s “First Take.”

On Nov. 4, when asked which AFC quarterback he would trust most in the playoffs, the college football analyst surprisingly picked Aaron, offering a positive nod to the Steelers star.

Aaron, meanwhile, has been gradually rebuilding ties across the family.

The quarterback reunited with his parents, Ed and Darla Rodgers, and older brother Luke in July.

He shared photos of the get-together on social media, describing the family as “bonding.” Jordan was noticeably missing from those pictures.

Aaron also appeared to take a swipe at his younger brother the following month, referencing Jordan’s decision to discuss their estrangement on “The Bachelorette” nearly a decade earlier.

But by September, Aaron was publicly confirming that the two had reconnected as he discussed repairing family ties ahead of his parents’ move from California to Nashville earlier this year.

“A couple weeks after that, I went out to Nashville and met with my older brother,” Aaron told the “Not Just Football” podcast, referring to Luke, who lives in Tennessee with his wife, Aimee, and their three children.

“A couple weeks after that, I met with my little brother. It was cool. There were tough conversations for sure, but I’m just in a much better headspace,” he revealed.

“Now, full circle, [we’re] back together. It’s amazing. It’s been great to have all those people — my little brother, my older brother and his family, my parents — that’s been really, really special,” Aaron added.

He also credited his wife, Brittani, for helping him reach a point where reconciliation felt possible.

“My wife deserves a lot of the credit for that just to be able to get to that point to think about having the conversations, she was a big part of that,” he said.
